Existing solutions either degrade accuracy through differential privacy or incur high computational and communication overhead with encryption. This paper proposes HEFedLoRA, a privacy-preserving federated LoRA framework that combines alternating aggregation with a threshold Paillier cryptosystem to securely aggregate the active low-rank factor in each round without revealing additional information about individual client updates beyond what can be inferred from the released aggregate factors. HEFedLoRA also eliminates aggregation discordance while supporting heterogeneous client ranks through a shared upper-rank alignment mechanism. Theoretical analysis proves security under the semi-honest model. Experiments show that HEFedLoRA retains 99.47% of the plaintext baseline accuracy, reduces server aggregation runtime by up to 28.5× relative to Se cLoRA, and approximately halves the communication overhead compared with naive encrypted baselines.
10.1109/ton.2026.3741719: Decentralized learning enhances privacy, scalability, and fault tolerance by distributing data and computation across nodes, making it a promising alternative to centralized approaches. Federated Learning, a widely adopted method, relies on a central aggregator but suffers from vulnerabilities such as single points of failure, limited scalability, and privacy risks. Gossip Learning and Epidemic Learning offer fully decentralized solutions through peer-to-peer exchanges of model updates, ensuring robustness and privacy but at the cost of slower convergence. In this work, we present HEAL, an innovative decentralized learning framework based on a self-organizing and self-healing Peer-to-Peer overlay. HEAL leverages emergent multi-hub networks, combining the randomness of graph structures with the efficiency of star networks. This architecture enables the organic formation of prominent hubs that enhance fault tolerance, reduce network diameter, and facilitate robust decentralized aggregation. HEAL is the first framework that integrates the strengths of Federated Learning, Gossip Learning, and Epidemic Learning, utilizing the Elevator algorithm to dynamically select aggregators. Our simulations demonstrate that HEAL outperforms Gossip Learning and Epidemic learning, and achieves performance comparable to Federated Learning in stable environments. These performances are maintained in scenarios with high node churn or network instability. This framework offers a scalable, privacy-preserving, and fault-tolerant solution for decentralized learning applications.
10.1109/tai.2026.3740663: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without sharing raw data, making it particularly suitable for smart agriculture, where data is sensitive and distributed across multiple stakeholders. However, FL introduces critical security vulnerabilities that can degrade model performance and compromise data confidentiality. This study investigates these vulnerabilities using real-world microclimate time series data from four greenhouses, representing distinct agricultural actors collaborating while retaining data locality. We study multiple adversarial attacks, including Data Poisoning, Backdoor, Model Update Poisoning, Property Inference, and Free Rider attacks, evaluating their impact on predictive performance and model reliability. To mitigate these threats, we evaluate multiple defense strategies, including Differential Privacy, Robust Aggregation, Quantization, Sparsification, Gradient Clipping, and Free Rider Detection mechanisms deployed at both client and server levels. Building on these existing mechanisms, we design a unified multi-layered defense pipeline that integrates data sanitization, adaptive clipping, Trust-Krum aggregation, and privacy-preserving noise injection into a single system-level framework. Experimental results demonstrate that this configuration achieves superior F1-Score across all attack scenarios while maintaining convergence stability. These findings underscore the necessity of integrated, synergistic defenses to ensure the secure and robust deployment of FL in adversarial environments.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3735015: Federated learning (FL) trains a global model by iteratively exchanging local model updates among clients, but poses challenges in terms of model convergence and system-wide energy consumption. To address these challenges when mobile devices (MDs) are spatially distributed, an FL framework for multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) with heterogeneous communication capacities is considered, where MD selection and UAV trajectories are jointly optimized. Specifically, each UAV serves as a UAV-base station (UAV-BS), equipped with a global machine learning model. In each round of the FL process, the MDs selected by the UAV-BSs can train their local FL model and upload the updated parameters of the model to their corresponding UAV. Hence, the MD selection strategy not only determines the performance of the global model, but also has a significant impact on the overall energy efficiency. Furthermore, since communication energy consumption depends on the positions of the UAV-BSs, it is essential to jointly optimize the MD selection and the UAV trajectories over all FL rounds. However, this long term multi-objective function constitutes a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, which is NP-hard and intractable. To address this challenge, a proximal policy optimization (PPO)-based reinforcement learning model under a centralized training and distributed execution (CTDE) framework is proposed. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively and jointly optimizes the MD selection and the UAV trajectories. Specifically, it outperforms benchmarks by optimizing the global model performance and the energy consumption, simultaneously.
10.1109/tccn.2026.3740672: Agentic AI systems are reshaping communications and networking by deploying autonomous intelligent agents capable of collaborative learning while maintaining data privacy at network edges. Within distributed network environments, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve as cognitive engines for edge devices, yet federated fine-tuning faces substantial challenges in balancing global knowledge aggregation with local adaptation under heterogeneous network conditions. Conventional federated protocols typically rely on uniform parameter aggregation, which conflates domain-invariant features with client-specific nuances, thereby resulting in suboptimal personalization and excessive communication overhead. To address these challenges, we propose PFAdapter, a communication-efficient framework introducing hierarchical LoRA decomposition to explicitly separate adapter parameters into global-shared and local-private components. Query and key projections are assigned to global synchronization for capturing universal multimodal semantics across the network, while value and output projections remain localized for edge-specific adaptation. Additionally, orthogonality regularization based on the Frobenius norm enforces strict separation between these components, preventing redundant feature learning. Selective aggregation protocols synchronize only global-shared components across the federated network, preserving local expertise and reducing communication costs by nearly 50%. Extensive experiments on VQA-RAD, SLAKE, Hateful Memes, and CrisisMMD datasets demonstrate that PFAdapter consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving accuracy improvements ranging from 2.4% to 4.8% across diverse edge intelligence tasks. Consequently, our framework establishes an efficient solution for agentic AI deployment in resource-constrained communication networks.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3740920: Privacy-preserving federated learning commonly adopts secure aggregation to hide individual updates; however, secure aggregation alone does not guarantee that an untrusted aggregation server aggregates the intended set of clients correctly under dynamic membership. This work presents EVA, an efficient framework for privacy-preserving and verifiable aggregation in federated learning. EVA decouples masked-update aggregation from masking-secret aggregation. Clients conceal local updates via a subset-sum-based masking mechanism and upload masked updates together with lightweight checksums to the aggregation server, while sending the corresponding auxiliary masking secrets to a trusted execution environment (TEE), which aggregates them. The server aggregates only masked updates and checksums, whereas the TEE aggregates the auxiliary secrets into a single secret state. Given the server output and the TEE-provided aggregated secret state, the clients participating in the next round can recover the unmasked aggregate and verify a single global consistency relation that binds the result to the aggregated checksum, thereby detecting deviation from correct aggregation except with negligible probability. EVA further supports anonymous yet authenticated participation via time-bound group signatures, enabling revocation and accountable traceability when required. We implement EVA in Go and Python and evaluate it on MNIST with MLP and CNN models. Experimental results show that EVA achieves model accuracy comparable to that of FedAvg while incurring low per-round overheads: the aggregation server remains lightweight even for large models, and the TEE overhead stays moderate, yielding substantial efficiency gains over representative baselines.
10.1109/tce.2026.3740732: Drone delivery networks require authorization across fleet-operator and civil-aviation domains and protected federated learning (FL) exchanges over wireless links. Concurrent associations require endpoint-specific keys and efficient protection of shared payloads. We present SMVAKA, a simultaneous multi-vertiport authentication and key-agreement protocol built from established primitives. Two non-colluding clouds process target-specific Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) shares as additive components. Sender-specific secrets reach authorized vertiports through an ECCDH-masked authenticated Invertible Bloom Lookup Table. The intersection of both cloud decisions determines accepted associations, whose endpoints combine these components into distinct keys. Neither cloud reconstructs an end-point key. Established epoch secrets support one protected broad-cast payload per sender and FL round. A Real-or-Random analysis establishes fresh-session key indistinguishability and single-cloud privacy under honest-but-curious clouds, and Colored Petri Nets verify the finite-state protocol flow. In the evaluated work-loads, SMVAKA reduced sender-side protection operation counts by a factor of nine relative to the repeated-pairwise baseline, with mean terminal-accuracy differences within 0.03 percentage points. Two authenticated recovery attempts achieved 99.58% key reconstruction at 10% effective loss. The measured per-target broadcast-size slope differed from the analytical prediction by 0.7%.
10.1109/tce.2026.3740729: Intelligent electric vehicles (EVs) are becoming high-value consumer electronic devices equipped with computation, sensing, and communication capabilities. However, using their idle vehicular computing capacity for federated intelligent services requires the simultaneous coordination of model architecture, hardware demand, owner incentives, and voluntary participation. These decisions are typically handled separately, which can lead to a mismatch between learning workloads and available resources and, consequently, unstable service provision. To address this problem, this paper proposes an architecture-aware dynamic matching and two-tier pricing framework that jointly considers model architecture, architecture-dependent hardware burden, owner response, and federated learning performance. Calibrated hardware profiles characterize device-specific latency, memory, communication, and energy demands; a Stackelberg pricing mechanism coordinates platform decisions with individually rational owner participation; and Hardware-Incentive-Coupled Evolutionary Federated Architecture Search (HIC-EvoFAS) performs feasibility-aware, multi-fidelity search over architecture and service decisions. The selected architecture reaches 89.12% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 93.78% on the German Traffic Sign Recognition Benchmark (GTSRB). Compared with federated neural architecture search (FedNAS), it reduces communication volume and round latency by 17.11% and 12.78%, respectively, while the proposed pricing mechanism improves platform utility by 58.90% over fixed pricing without revenue sharing. These results show that incorporating hardware requirements and owner incentives directly into architecture selection can improve both federated learning performance and the practical use of distributed vehicular computing capacity resources.
10.1109/tase.2026.3740234: Cross-scenario collaborative trajectory planning can improve Automated Valet Parking (AVP) by transferring policy knowledge learned from vehicle experiences in different environments. However, existing transfer approaches often rely on static architectures, coarse representations, and limited adaptability, restricting continual knowledge sharing across heterogeneous scenarios. We propose a Self-Organizing Federated Reinforcement Learning (SO-FRL) framework for cloud-edge-vehicle collaboration. The vehicle layer performs local perception and real-time planning, the edge layer aggregates vehicle-level knowledge into parking-lot repositories, and the cloud layer integrates multi-scenario knowledge for cross-scenario generalization. SO-FRL combines a self-organizing network with federated node-level knowledge transfer, enabling continual policy evolution without directly sharing raw trajectories or sensor streams. Experiments in controlled simulations constructed from multiple real parking-lot maps show that SO-FRL achieves the highest measured success rate and success-weighted path efficiency among the tested learning-based and classical baselines, reaching$79.0\% \pm 1.5\%$SR and$0.60 \pm 0.04$SPL. It also yields lower and more consistent navigation error while maintaining a compact knowledge structure and acceptable computational complexity. Note to Practitioners—This paper introduces an SO-FRL framework for cross-scenario trajectory planning and adaptive knowledge sharing in autonomous valet parking. By continually compressing and evolving a cloud-edge-vehicle node-based knowledge repository, SO-FRL is designed to reduce onboard model size and uplink traffic by exchanging compact knowledge nodes rather than raw trajectories or raw sensor streams. The current evaluation is conducted in a controlled simulator built from real parking-lot map files, including parking-space layouts, lane geometry, drivable boundaries, and entrance/exit markers. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as real-map-based algorithmic validation rather than field-deployment evidence. The present study does not yet include real-vehicle experiments, digital-twin deployment, or validation in a high-fidelity sensor/traffic simulator. Communication delay and packet loss, unstable edge connectivity, localization error, sensor noise, dynamic pedestrian behavior, unexpected obstacles, cybersecurity risks, and edge-server failures remain to be evaluated in future deployment-oriented validation.
10.1109/tase.2026.3740530: This study presents FedSSL-ADIM, a privacy-preserving federated semi-supervised framework for industrial machine vision that addresses data-centralization constraints, high annotation costs, and cross-site heterogeneity. Deployed across three textile factories with 80 robotic systems and edge devices rated at 0.1–1.0 TFLOPS, the framework combines a novel Adaptive Data-Driven Aggregation (ADDA) mechanism, online incremental updates, and differential privacy. ADDA weights client updates using dataset size, labeled-data fraction, and pseudo-label entropy to mitigate non-IID effects. The system achieved a mean average precision (mAP) of 0.984 for Empty Pocket Detection (EPD) and an accuracy of 0.994 for Bobbin Head-Tail Identification (BHTI). At Factory C, the most heterogeneous site (61.4% contamination; 0.1 TFLOPS), ADDA improved mAP by 7.4 percentage points (8.2% relative) over the FL+SSL baseline (0.901 to 0.975). Annotation costs fell by 90%, and the differential privacy mechanism provided formal guarantees with only 0.2–0.5% mAP degradation. In a three-month operational evaluation, production efficiency increased by 8.1–12.3%, false positives decreased by 12.9–18.2%, and downtime decreased by 18.7–22.1%. The economic analysis showed a$4.0\times $return on investment and a 2.3-month payback period. The results support privacy-compliant, annotation-efficient federated vision as a replicable approach for heterogeneous industrial settings. Note to Practitioners—Textile factories can use FedSSL-ADIM to improve visual inspection across sites without sharing raw production images. This is useful when privacy regulations (e.g., PIPL and GDPR), limited bandwidth, or sparse labels make centralized training difficult. Field-tested across three factories operating 80 robotic systems, the framework runs on industrial PCs with 0.1–1.0 TFLOPS and supports Empty Pocket Detection (EPD) and Bobbin Head-Tail Identification (BHTI). It achieved 0.984 mAP and 0.994 accuracy, respectively. The ADDA mechanism weights each site’s model updates according to dataset size, labeled-data fraction, and pseudo-label entropy, reducing the influence of unreliable data and addressing site heterogeneity. It reduced manual labeling effort by 90% and improved production efficiency by 8.1–12.3%. At the most heterogeneous factory, ADDA raised mAP by 7.4 percentage points (8.2% relative) over the FL+SSL baseline. Differential privacy ($\epsilon = 5.0$,$\delta = 3\times 10^{-3}$) caused 0.2–0.5% mAP degradation. During a three-month evaluation, false positives decreased by 12.9–18.2%, downtime by 18.7–22.1%, and net savings totaled${\$}62.2$K, corresponding to a$4.0\times $return on investment and a 2.3-month payback. The architecture is designed to work with existing industrial protocols. The reported system meets a 400-ms production cycle, with inference latencies of 42–187 ms for EPD and 68–312 ms for BHTI. Further work should reduce latency for faster lines and evaluate multimodal inputs such as vibration and acoustic signals. A three-slide multimedia deck illustrating deployment is provided as supplementary material.
arxiv:2610.21969: The convergence of communication and computation, empowered by artificial intelligence (AI) enhanced capabilities, emerges as a key enabler for realizing the promising functionalities of the sixth-generation of communication systems (6G). To this end, this paper investigates an AI-native, robust network, where multiple base stations (BSs) simultaneously serve several extended reality (XR) devices. The paper then presents an innovative distributed deep learning-based approach to simultaneously manage the transmit and computing powers, and computation allocation, amidst uncertainties in both channel and computing states information. Under such an interference network scenario, the paper proposes a robust approach for minimizing the worst-case delay across the served XR devices, subject to computation and power constraints. The paper leverages a deep neural network (DNN) that can be trained either centrally or in a federated manner to map estimated channels and computation requirements to optimized resource allocations per BS. During training, uncertainty samples, reflecting both channel and computing estimation errors, are injected after the DNN output to account for such joint uncertainties. Our results validate the enhanced robust delay performance and scalability of joint uncertainty injection as compared to uncertainty-agnostic methods and state-of-the-art benchmarks, with federated learning-based solutions achieving near-centralized performance while enhancing efficiency, privacy, and adaptability.
10.1109/tnsm.2026.3739767: With the increasing demand for privacy and distributed data compliance, federated learning (FL) has become a promising paradigm for collaborative network traffic classification (NTC) without sharing raw traffic data. However, real-world network environments are inherently open, where the emergence of new applications and unknown attacks introduces open-set challenges. To ensure service quality and network security, models need not only to classify known traffic classes accurately but also to identify unknown ones. Despite recent efforts to extend FL to Open-Set NTC (OSNTC), most current FL methods are still confined to the closed-set assumption, leaving the challenge of Federated OSNTC (FedOSNTC) largely unresolved. Therefore, this paper proposes FedUTD, a novel Federated Unknown Traffic Detection framework that introduces: 1) multi-scale prefix truncation, a customized contrastive learning strategy that leverages multi-granularity traffic characteristics to enhance feature discriminability; 2) an improved federated communication mechanism that enriches the transmitted information through pseudo-sample generation to mitigate data heterogeneity while retaining substantially lower communication cost; and 3) a lightweight dual-layer OSNTC approach designed to reduce local training and inference overhead during local unknown-traffic detection. Extensive experiments on four real-world network traffic datasets demonstrate that FedUTD consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving an F1 gain of 5–21%.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3740159: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) based on low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables mobile devices with multi-task datasets to collaboratively fine-tune a large language model (LLM) by exchanging locally updated parameters with a subset of neighboring devices via wireless connections for knowledge integration.However, directly aggregating parameters fine-tuned on heterogeneous datasets induces three primary issues across the DFL life-cycle: (i) \textit{catastrophic knowledge forgetting during fine-tuning process}, arising from conflicting update directions caused by data heterogeneity; (ii) \textit{inefficient communication and convergence during model aggregation process}, due to bandwidth-intensive redundant model transmissions; and (iii) \textit{multi-task knowledge interference during inference process}, resulting from incompatible knowledge representations coexistence during inference. To address these issues in a fully decentralized scenario, we first propose a sparse-and-orthogonal LoRA that ensures orthogonality between model updates to eliminate direction conflicts during fine-tuning.Then, we analyze how device connection topology affects multi-task performance, prompting a cluster-based topology design during aggregation.Finally, we propose an implicit mixture of experts (MoE) mechanism to avoid the coexistence of incompatible knowledge during inference. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively reduces communication resource consumption by up to $73\%$ and enhances average performance by $5\%$ compared with the traditional LoRA method.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3739774: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across multiple parties without sharing raw local data, and has been widely deployed in healthcare, finance, and in dustrial IoT scenarios. Existing privacy-preserving FL methods mainly rely on differential privacy, secure aggregation, and homomorphic encryption, offering diverse degrees of defense against gradient leakage and model-inversion attacks. However, in practical edge deployments, rational, resource-constrained clients may intentionally cut down local training efforts. Such client behavior slows convergence, hurts model performance, and raises cumulative system costs throughout training. Furthermore, prevailing privacy mechanisms introduce non-negligible computational and communication overhead, which aggravates energy consumption. To resolve these issues and coordinate autonomous client decisions under privacy and resource constraints, we propose FedPGame, a potential game-based federated learning framework. Specifically, we model privacy-aware local strategy selection as a finite non-cooperative potential game, enabling clients to autonomously choose their resource-investment levels. We further devise a heterogeneity-aware client-level cost function together with its corresponding global potential function. This design aligns unilateral client-side cost reduction with global potential descent and guarantee convergence to a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. Differential privacy is incorporated through an explicit training-horizon (ε,δ)-DP upper bound and a pre scribed DP-budget constraint. Solid theoretical analysis and comprehensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that FedPGame achieves a favorable trade-off among privacy protection, client autonomy, model utility, and energy efficiency.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3739657: Movement trajectory similarity learning supports many transportation applications, such as trajectory retrieval, route analysis, and anomaly detection. In practice, trajectories are increasingly collected by distributed mobile and edge devices rather than stored at a central location. Federated learning enables collaborative training without directly sharing raw trajectories, but differences among client data can reduce model performance. Existing solutions also face challenges in privacypreserving client clustering and usually require separate models for different trajectory similarity relations. To address these problems, we propose P-FLITS, a privacy-preserving federated framework for multi-relation trajectory similarity learning. PFLITS separates public road representation from private trajectory processing and transfers multiple knowledge of trajectory relations into one compact Student model. It further uses trajectory-level differential privacy for client clustering, together with shuffled reporting and secure aggregation to protect client reports and model updates. Formal security analysis shows that P-FLITS provides trajectory-level differential privacy for routeprofile reporting, client-report unlinkability under the shuffling assumptions, and confidentiality of individual model updates under secure aggregation. Experiments on T-Drive, Porto, and GeoLife show that, compared with the closely related F-TSL scheme, P-FLITS achieves better retrieval performance in 46 of 48 evaluated settings, with an average absolute improvement of 17.5 percentage points.
10.1109/twc.2026.3739110: The use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to facilitate federated learning (FL) has attracted growing attention, as UAVs can mitigate key limitations of terrestrial FL systems by enabling reliable participation of devices located at the network edge. This capability is particularly important for FL systems employing over-the-air (OTA) aggregation, where devices experiencing weak wireless channels can severely distort the aggregated updates. However, the limited coverage of UAVs introduces staleness issues, since devices may not be able to participate synchronously, leading to degraded learning performance. To address these challenges, we propose a staleness-aware UAV-assisted OTA asynchronous FL framework that jointly optimizes transceiver design, device scheduling, and UAV trajectory. We first establish a convergence analysis that explicitly characterizes the impact of staleness on learning performance. Building on this analysis, we formulate a joint optimization problem that minimizes the performance loss due to staleness and OTA communication errors. We propose an alternating optimization algorithm to solve this problem, and analyze its convergence and computational complexity. To cope with time-varying wireless fading in practical UAV operations, we further propose an online transceiver adjustment mechanism that dynamically refines the transceiver parameters during FL execution. Extensive simulation results based on benchmark learning datasets demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves faster convergence and higher accuracy than existing schemes.
10.1109/tnsm.2026.3738968: The increasing deployment of Internet of Things (IoT) applications has created a growing need for distributed learning frameworks that can operate efficiently across resource-constrained edge environments while preserving data privacy. Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without sharing raw data. However, its communication overhead, computational burden, and limited scalability make it less suitable for large-scale hierarchical edge networks. In this paper, we propose Hierarchical Federated Split Learning (HFSL), a unified (UAV)-assisted edge-fog-cloud framework that combines the complementary strengths of FL and Split Learning (SL) to improve communication efficiency, scalability, and privacy. HFSL introduces activation similarity-based clustering and spatio-temporal activation filtering to reduce redundant communication, adaptive UAV altitude optimization to improve wireless connectivity under dynamic network conditions, and a privacy-preserving training strategy based on Differential Privacy (DP) and activation-level leakage mitigation. Extensive experiments across eight image and tabular benchmark datasets demonstrate that HFSL outperforms state-of-the-art FL and SL methods on the more challenging heterogeneous benchmarks, reducing energy consumption by up to 50%, training latency by 40%, and communication overhead by 35%, while improving classification accuracy by up to 6%. These results show that HFSL provides an effective and scalable distributed learning framework for next-generation UAV-assisted edge networks.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3739043: Recent advancements in Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) have introduced a transformative approach, enabling organizations with limited and fragmented datasets to collaboratively train machine learning models and enhance data utility. Meanwhile, the tightening of global data privacy regulations-driven by heightened concerns over data breaches and information leakage-has spurred the development of numerous privacy-preserving VFL frameworks. Among these, boosting algorithms have emerged as particularly promising due to their flexibility and wide-ranging applicability. Although several privacy-preserving approaches to Adaptive Boosting (AdaBoost) have been investigated, AdaBoost training specifically within the VFL framework remains largely underexplored. Furthermore, existing VFL solutions based on tree-boosting methods often exhibit suboptimal performance when adapted to the AdaBoost paradigm. To address this gap, we propose an efficient and privacy-preserving AdaBoost training framework for VFL. Our approach introduces a packing technique based on symmetric homomorphic encryption (SHE) to reduce communication overhead. Additionally, we design secure sub-protocols for batch data comparison and minimum value computation, enabling confidential generation of prediction labels and the secure selection of the optimal weak classifier in each training round. These components collectively form the foundation of our VFL AdaBoost training framework. Our security analysis confirms that our scheme ensures privacy guarantees under the honest-but-curious model. Experimental evaluations further demonstrate that our framework not only achieves high accuracy, but also maintains superior computational and communication efficiency when compared to existing baseline methods.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3739050: Federated Recommender Systems (FedRecs) have gained significant traction as a privacy-preserving paradigm, enabling the collaborative training of global models without exchanging raw user data. Despite these advancements, standard FedRec models remain susceptible to attribute inference attacks, where adversaries can exploit shared embeddings to recover sensitive demographic information such as gender and race. To mitigate this risk, we propose targeting these specific features through federated unlearning. We introduce Aegis, a novel post-training framework designed to selectively purge sensitive attributes from user embeddings, thereby thwarting inference attacks while preserving recommendation utility. Technically, Aegis leverages embedding disentanglement to separate sensitive features from general preference information, using an information-theoretic multi-component loss function to optimize the balance between privacy protection and model performance. Crucially, our framework is capable of operating without access to original training interaction data through autonomous client-side protection. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that Aegis effectively safeguards user privacy with minimal degradation in recommendation accuracy.
10.1109/tsg.2026.3738792: The rapid growth of AI and cloud services has transformed data centers into geographically distributed, highly dynamic electrical loads whose behavior increasingly influences bulk power system reliability and renewable energy integration. In parallel, emerging interest in pairing data centers with hybrid on-site energy resources provides access to dispatchable supply and fast flexibility, but also introduces tightly coupled IT–thermal–electrical dynamics and hard operational limits that are not captured by conventional planning or control models. This paper presents a hierarchical coordination framework that integrates an MILP expansion model with physics-constrained reinforcement learning (RL) for the integrated planning and operation of emerging data center networks. The upper level cooptimizes site selection, IT and storage capacities and inter-site bandwidth, guided by flexibility envelopes and reliability metrics extracted from the lower level. The lower level employs a physics-constrained proximal policy optimization (PC-PPO) algorithm with federated parameter aggregation, enabling local agents to satisfy system-level constraints without sharing proprietary operational data. Simulations on a modified IEEE 118-bus system with realistic workload traces and renewable profiles underscore the importance of embedding operational feasibility and control into expansion planning for next-generation grid-interactive data centers.
10.1109/tce.2026.3738403: Connected and autonomous consumer vehicles face escalating cybersecurity threats as their attack surfaces expand through Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication, over-the-air (OTA) updates, and complex electronic architectures. Threat Analysis and Risk Assessment (TARA), mandated by ISO/SAE 21434, is essential for systematic threat mitigation, yet many automated TARA pipelines still rely on tree-structured threat models that fail to capture shared attack paths, on rule-based or LLM-driven reasoning without graph-structural learning, and on black-box risk scoring that lacks the traceability expected for safety-critical systems. Attack-graph–based automotive TARA has been studied for more than a decade (e.g., MulVAL, CarVal, GAPP, THREATGET); our contribution is not to introduce attack graphs to this area, but to integrateunifiedgraph construction, multi-task Graph Attention Network (GAT) inference, and a layered explanation mechanism into a single learnable pipeline. In this paper, we propose AG-TARA, which combines attack graph modeling, Graph Attention Networks (GAT), and a three-level explainable AI architecture for automotive cybersecurity assessment: it first constructs a unified attack graph from vehicle configuration data, vulnerability databases, and standardized attack pattern repositories to enable node sharing and edge reuse across threat scenarios; a multi-head GAT-based risk inference engine then learns structural attack patterns for simultaneous node risk classification and attack path prediction; finally, a three-level explainability architecture combining attention weight visualization, GNNExplainer-based feature attribution, and attack path contribution analysis provides traceable risk explanations aligned with the auditability principles of ISO/SAE 21434. Extensive experiments on a real-world automotive cybersecurity dataset demonstrate that AG-TARA achieves 82.35% accuracy and 0.8367 Macro-F1 in risk classification and 0.9873 AUC in attack path prediction, matching or exceeding state-of-the-art GNN and LLM-based baselines while reducing per-scenario analysis time by over 97% compared to LLM-agent methods. We additionally outline a federated AG-TARA deployment mode and report a small-scale FedAvg experiment as a preliminary validation; full federated deployment remains future work.
10.1109/taslpro.2026.3739189: Existing audio backdoor attacks typically rely on injecting perceptible triggers, such as additive noise or fixed signals, making them susceptible to detection. This paper introduces a more covert paradigm: Transformation-based Instancedependent Backdoor Attacks (TIBA). Rather than inserting external triggers, TIBA leverages common audio quality transformations- such as low-bitrate compression and interpolation-as implicit, instance-specific attack vectors. By applying controlled degradations to individual training samples and assigning them malicious target labels, the model is induced to learn spurious correlations between subtle quality cues and target predictions. Unlike fixed triggers that tend to induce overfitting, TIBA's instance-specific quality transformations introduce diverse trigger patterns across samples, thereby increasing stealth against detection methods that rely on recognizing consistent activation signatures.Without introducing FL-specific update manipulation, we further evaluate whether this local data-poisoning mechanism remains effective under robust aggregation rules. Extensive experiments on speech command and speaker recognition datasets confirm that TIBA achieves high attack success rates in both digital and physical environments while preserving clean accuracy. This study broadens the investigation of compressionbased audio backdoors to a unified set of directly deployable compression and resampling transformations, with particular emphasis on their input-dependent artifacts and empirical behavior under robust federated aggregation. Our code is available athttps://github.com/Maozhen-Zhang/TIBA.git.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3738635: Conventional patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), such as the Physical Activity Scale for the Elderly (PASE), are prone to recall bias and subjectivity, particularly in older adults. To mitigate these issues, we propose ActiCare, a framework for automated PASE assessment. Data are integrated from heterogeneous non-intrusive sensors to generate uncertainty-quantified activity labels under a federated learning paradigm. The perception module includes Shapley-guided model selection, representation-aware aggregation, and confidence-aware decision-level fusion, providing structured activity labels and confidence estimates for downstream reasoning. The perception module handles partially missing modalities through calibrated fusion. A multi-stage assessment plan preserves unavailable or persistently low-confidence segments as flagged uncertainty records and analyzes temporal patterns to infer composite activities. These activity labels are incrementally summarized across temporal scales, with the process guided by a scale-oriented knowledge base of PASE definitions and scoring rules. A frozen large language model (LLM) applies rule-guided reasoning to generate both the final PASE scores and corresponding narrative reports. In controlled synthetic week-long activity trajectories constructed from the XRF-55 benchmark, ActiCare achieves higher rubric-based scoring-compliance and scoring-accuracy scores than LLM-only prompting without explicit PASE rule grounding. A one-week rehabilitation-ward deployment with 12 inpatients demonstrates close agreement with clinician scoring (MAE = 4.5, MAPE = 6.8%, ICC(2,1) = 0.90).
10.1109/tsp.2026.3738791: This work addresses the key challenges of applying federated learning to large-scale deep neural networks, particularly the issue of client drift due to data heterogeneity across clients and the high costs of communication, computation, and memory. We propose FedSub, an efficient subspace algorithm for federated learning on heterogeneous data. Specifically, FedSub utilizes subspace projection to guarantee local updates of each client within low-dimensional subspaces, thereby reducing communication, computation, and memory costs. Additionally, it incorporates low-dimensional dual variables to mitigate client drift. We provide convergence analysis that reveals the impact of key factors such as step size and subspace projection matrices on convergence. Experimental results demonstrate its efficiency.
10.1109/tcomm.2026.3738508: Federated learning (FL) facilitates knowledge interaction among agents (both spatially and temporally) by keeping raw data on-device and exchanging only model updates, thereby improving localization performance for multi-agent systems. However, existing FL-based localization models typically lack the capability to capture agent-specific features and require substantial computation and communication resources, limiting their effectiveness and widespread adoption. To address these challenges, we propose a lightweight personalized federated learning (LPFL) approach for spatial and temporal multi-agent interactive localization (MAIL). Specifically, each agent maintains a local localization model while the central server manages a global one. During each round, agents adapt the broadcast global model with local training data, compute validation gradients, and upload them for server aggregation. This validation-guided update enables LPFL to enhance both personalization and cross-agent generalization, improving cooperative localization accuracy. Additionally, adaptive model pruning and gradient quantization are implemented to compress the model, aiming at improving the computational and communication efficiencies for multi-agent systems. Theoretical analyses validate the training performance and efficiency of LPFL, making it a feasible and reliable framework for MAIL. Finally, we conduct comprehensive real-world experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of LPFL.
10.1109/ton.2026.3738131: Despite the structural advantages for privacy in federated learning (FL), many gradient inversion attacks have widely appeared to endanger the privacy of participants, by exploiting the information during communications. This is still valid for the case where FL is extended to quantum FL (QFL) to utilize quantum advantages. To deal with the privacy leakage during communications, quantum teleportation (QT) can be adopted to QFL for ensuring privacy during communications, by hiding the important information from outsiders. However, it should also address (i) the threats due to privacy attacks from insiders and (ii) the communication efficiency with QT. To tackle these issues, this paper proposes novel QFL adopting quantum local differential privacy (Q-LDP), which is the extension of differential privacy to quantum domains for both communication efficiency and privacy. The proposed algorithm shows privacy and utility enhancement compared to baselines, in terms of reduced attacks and maximized communication efficiency.
10.1109/tcyb.2026.3735876: Federated learning (FL) becomes highly vulnerable when adversaries manipulate multiple evidence channels simultaneously, especially under nonindependent and identically distributed (non-IID) data distributions that allow attackers to bypass gradient-only defenses. Existing robust aggregation methods are designed for isolated single-channel attacks and fail to account for interactions across labels, features, and gradients. To address this limitation, we develop a composite attack model that captures coordinated multichannel manipulation, characterizing how cross-channel interactions create amplification and masking effects that render single-view defenses ineffective. We then propose a multiview interaction-aware defense (MVIAD) that evaluates each client through an interaction consistency score (ICS) derived from label, feature, and gradient deviations, complemented by a temporal reputation mechanism for persistent behavioral assessment. Our theoretical analysis proves that composite attacks induce strictly larger model divergence than any single-channel attack under equal budgets, and that MVIAD converges to a bounded robustness region even with adversarial contamination. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and NSL-KDD confirm the severity of composite attacks, where baseline methods lose over 40% accuracy and exhibit attack success rates (ASRs) exceeding 80% under high malicious rates. On the contrary, MVIAD maintains high robustness, achieving 93.9% accuracy on MNIST, 63.5% on CIFAR-10% and 97.8% on NSL-KDD under 40% composite attacks, keeping ASR below 15% for NSL-KDD, outperforming state-of-the-art defenses.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3738647: Vertical federated learning (VFL) is a privacy-preserving distributed learning paradigm in which multiple edge parties share aligned samples but hold different feature subsets, and collaboratively train a model without exchanging their raw data. Despite its practical importance, vertical federated unlearning (VFU), which aims to remove the influence of designated features from a trained VFL model, remains insufficiently studied. It is important for privacy-driven feature revocation and the removal of malicious knowledge. Existing VFL unlearning methods require access to complete training information, such as full feature sets, labels or model parameters, and are primarily evaluated under a single VFL architecture. These limitations hinder their applicability to heterogeneous VFL systems. To address these limitations, we propose a unified unlearning framework for heterogeneous VFL systems comprising two complementary modules: Lipschitz-Based Feature Unlearning (LFU) and Model-Agnostic Knowledge Transfer (MAKT). Leveraging Lipschitz continuity, LFU formulates unsupervised feature unlearning in Aggregation-based VFL through a dual-mask optimization mechanism. To handle model-incomplete Split-based VFL scenarios, MAKT introduces an embedding-based knowledge distillation strategy that enables model-agnostic knowledge transfer without requiring access to the complete model. The proposed unlearning framework allows edge nodes to trigger feature unlearning on demand without retraining or interrupting other edge nodes. Extensive experiments on two representative unlearning tasks across six real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves precise feature removal under both VFL architectures, while outperforming existing baselines in unlearning efficiency.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3737851: Federated edge learning (FEEL) enables multiple devices to collaboratively train a global machine learning model through periodic parameter exchanges with the server. However, channel heterogeneity and unreliability across devices remain critical bottlenecks that significantly hinder the convergence of FEEL. To tackle this issue, one feasible approach is to employ reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) to reshape the wireless propagation environment and improve communication reliability. Nonetheless, sensing, computation, and communication jointly affect learning performance while competing for limited system resources such as bandwidth, latency, and energy budget, resulting in strong coupling among these processes in RIS-FEEL systems. To address these challenges, this paper investigates an RIS-assisted FEEL system with integrated sensing, computation, and communication (ISCC). Specifically, we theoretically derive an upper bound on the convergence gap for the RIS-FEEL system under model transmission error, which characterizes the impact of device scheduling and ISCC factors on learning performance. Guided by these theoretical insights, we further formulate a joint optimization problem to accelerate FEEL convergence under system resource constraints. To solve the resulting non-convex problem, we develop a block coordinate descent (BCD) method to alternately optimize transmit power, bandwidth allocation, device scheduling, sensing batch size, and RIS configuration. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme outperforms the benchmark schemes in terms of convergence rate and learning accuracy.
10.1109/tnnls.2026.3735731: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without sharing raw data, but its robustness is vulnerable to Byzantine clients, especially under non-identically distributed (non-IID) data. In heterogeneous FL, benign client updates may become multimodal and statistically diverse, making it difficult for majority-based defenses to distinguish malicious deviations from legitimate client diversity. Reference-based defenses, on the other hand, may suffer from distributional mismatch and often require trusted server data. To address these challenges, we propose Z-score and Minkowski distance-based aggregation with multihead self-attention (ZMASA), a two-stage Byzantine-robust aggregation framework for non-IID FL. In the first stage, ZMASA performs dimension-wise Z-score normalization on client update residuals, partitions clients into hierarchical confidence groups, and validates groups using a high-order Minkowski-distance criterion. This design suppresses coordinated malicious updates without requiring prior knowledge of the Byzantine ratio. In the second stage, ZMASA applies multihead self-attention (MHSA) to the retained candidate updates to adaptively assign aggregation weights and accommodate heterogeneous honest behaviors. We provide a theoretical analysis showing that, under bounded retained residuals, the aggregation error is controlled by the candidate-set Byzantine contamination, the magnitude of retained Byzantine residuals, and the stability of attention weights. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, AG-News, and CIFAR-100 under diverse Byzantine attacks and non-IID settings demonstrate that ZMASA achieves competitive or superior robustness compared with classical and recent robust aggregation baselines. Ablation, parameter sensitivity, scalability, and efficiency studies further validate the effectiveness and practicality of the proposed design.
10.1109/taes.2026.3738067: Federated global navigation satellite system (GNSS) monitoring distributes a proprietary classifier to partly trusted stations, any of which may leak its copy. ZK-Trace combines public identity marks, recipient-specific Tardos fingerprints, and zero-knowledge credential verification. The registry supports offline tracing without the leaker's cooperation. We establish conditional false-accusation bounds for arbitrary recovered bit patterns, a finite completeness bound under a hidden-bias residual channel, and a deterministic tracing-score bound for correlated feature-distillation errors. An interval-arithmetic checker makes the conditional bound executable and allocates a common budget across accusation and tamper decisions. Under innocent-row independence, the certificate-based evaluation uses a false-naming budget of 0.001 per investigation. It isolates all 160 single-owner copies and traces 712 of 720 two-owner mixtures without naming an innocent. Experiments use a simulated GNSS federation and CIFAR-10. Feature matching preserves the feature mark in 20/20 runs and cross-architecture transfer in 19/20, at copy-accuracy costs of 4.8 and 6.1 percentage points on GNSS and CIFAR-10. Function-only distillation erases the feature mark, and distillation also removes weight-space marks. These results support verifiable tracing under explicit statistical and cryptographic assumptions. Credential knowledge and recipient evidence serve distinct roles.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3737743: Federated learning, emerging as a new paradigm in distributed learning, effectively mitigates data leakage by exchanging model parameters instead of raw data. Without the intervention of blockchain, the primary challenge in conventional federated learning lies in the inherent risks of data privacy breaches and the inefficiency in managing and securing the distributed learning process, significantly impacting the overall model performance and reliability. This paper introduces a decentralized federated learning framework, designated as Federated Scoring Consensus (FSC), which amalgamates blockchain technology with a reputation-based incentive mechanism. Initially, we developed an innovative decentralized validation mechanism, fortified by the election of proxy servers, to efficaciously prevent single-node failures, thereby enhancing system robustness. Subsequently, the framework integrates blockchain technology to securely protect model updates submitted by mobile devices, ensuring both safety and reliability in the updating process. Furthermore, the influence of malicious nodes is mitigated through an incentive mechanism, which also expels them from the network when necessary, while simultaneously encouraging legitimate devices to contribute higher quality model updates. Comprehensive experiments conducted on public datasets, MNIST and CIFAR-10, corroborate the efficacy of the FSC framework. The results demonstrate not only an improvement in overall model performance but also an augmentation in the system's resilience against attacks and protection of data privacy.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3737783: Federated Recommendation (FedRec) systems en able decentralized training of personalized recommendation models to mitigate privacy concerns. However, recent studies reveal their vulnerability to interaction-level membership in ference attacks. Existing attacks, such as IMIA, rely on the unrealistic assumption of knowing the system's negative sampling ratio, limiting their practicality. In this work, we propose T LiRA, a knowledge-free inference framework that exploits the intrinsic correlation between the optimization trajectory and interaction labels. T-LiRA eliminates the dependency on prior knowledge via a novel “propose-and-verify” paradigm. It first performs a coarse-grained clustering of item updates to establish a global context, followed by a fine-grained, item-wise two tailed likelihood ratio test. This test evaluates the directional alignment between the real item updates and simulated updates generated under conflicting label hypotheses. By focusing on the direction rather than the magnitude of updates, T-LiRA achieves robust inference even in the presence of clustering noise or varying gradient scales. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that T-LiRA achieves a 2× higher F1 score compared to state-of-the-art methods in knowledge-free settings and remains effective against defenses such as Local Differential Privacy (LDP) and regularization.
10.1109/tce.2026.3737469: The rapid growth of latency-sensitive applications, particularly within consumer electronics, has accelerated the adoption of edge–cloud computing, yet dynamic bandwidth allocation remains a persistent challenge for delivering robust quality of service (QoS) in mobile edge environments. Existing approaches often rely on centralized control, optimize isolated performance metrics, and fail to align user QoS requirements with provider incentives. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Utility-oriented Bandwidth Allocation via Auction Mechanisms (UBAAM), a decentralized framework that integrates auction-theoretic modeling, QoS-aware resource orchestration, and federated learning. UBAAM employs a multi-dimensional utility formulation and a dual-price adjustment mechanism to balance user demand and provider profitability. At the same time, a Lyapunov optimization-based equilibrium ensures system stability under time-varying workloads. A privacy-preserving federated learning module further enhances bid prediction accuracy without sharing sensitive data, and a priority-aware auction supports multi-class bandwidth allocation. Experimental results on a real-world edge–cloud platform show that UBAAM improves bandwidth utilization by 14%-33%, reduces carbon emissions by 19.4%, increases provider revenue by 88.5%, and lowers user costs by 31.9%, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving QoS, resource efficiency, and economic sustainability.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3737460: Federated Learning (FL), although designed to protect raw data privacy, remains vulnerable to model poisoning attacks due to its reliance on client-provided model updates. However, existing poisoning methods typically require access to client-side information or rely on restrictive assumptions, limiting their practicality in realistic, data-constrained environments. This raises the need for adaptive and data-free poisoning strategies that operate without access to client data. In this work, we introduce FedFree, a data-free model poisoning framework that requires only the sequence of server-broadcast global parameters. Its core is a history-guided inversion mechanism: FedFree estimates benign update statistics from the public global-model trajectory and shapes malicious updates that approximate benign client dynamics, reinforced by multi-source perturbation injection and an adaptive norm-clipping controller. Within its benign-update simulator, a block-wise, Shampoo-style second-order preconditioner is adopted as a numerical-stability enhancement rather than the primary source of attack effectiveness. Extensive experiments across three datasets and eleven aggregation strategies (including the FedAvg no-defense baseline) show that, under sustained adversarial participation, FedFree delivers the strongest degradation among all compared attacks under Multi-Krum, Trimmed-mean, and FLShield, ranks second or third under FedAvg, CC, RFA, RoFL, and FedGT, and is most strongly suppressed by the similarity- and projection-based defenses FoolsGold and DnC. We further analyze the quality of the generated benign simulation module. The surrogate updates exhibit high statistical consistency with real client updates, achieving cosine similarity above 0.993 and norm ratios close to 1.0 under different data heterogeneity settings. Ablation studies further show that history/trajectory modeling is the dominant driver of attack effectiveness, while the Shampoo-style design mainly improves numerical stability while preserving overall attack behavior.
10.1109/tkde.2026.3734471: Detecting fraud in cryptocurrency networks re quires a view of transaction activity that crosses organizational boundaries, yet centralizing that data would undermine the confidentiality that decentralized ledgers are designed to protect. Prior work addresses the capabilities this problem demands (temporal graph learning, federated collaboration, and differential privacy) separately, and none combines them under a single formal guarantee. This paper presents TEMPURA, a framework that unifies all three. Temporal Neighborhood Privacy (TNP) calibrates noise to a smooth upper bound on a node's temporally weighted sensitivity; at the operating point this reduces the noise standard deviation by a factor of 4.8 (a 79% reduction) relative to the standard Gaussian mechanism under the same (ϵ, δ) guarantee. Provably Robust Federated Graph Aggregation (PRFGA) pairs a coordinate-wise trimmed mean, whose exact replace-one sensitivity we derive, with spectral outlier screening; it converges at O(1/√KT) to a neighborhood of a stationary point whose radius scales with the corruption level, and retains F1 = 0.82 against the strongest adaptive attack at 30% Byzantine participation. Adaptive Temporal Discrepancy Learning (ATDL) attends to fraud at four timescales and encodes directional node pair asymmetries. On four transaction datasets (up to 203M edges), TEMPURA attains F1 = 0.9012 without privacy and F1 = 0.8654 under ϵ = 1.0 federated privacy, a 3.6-point degradation, while significantly outperforming every federated baseline.
10.1109/tkde.2026.3736353: Federated learning systems are increasingly threatened by data poisoning attacks, where malicious clients compromise global models by contributing tampered updates. Existing defenses often rely on impractical assumptions, such as access to a central test dataset, or fail to generalize across diverse attack types, particularly those involving multiple malicious clients working collaboratively. To address this, we propose Federated Noise-Induced Activation Analysis (FedNIA), a novel defense framework to identify and exclude adversarial clients without relying on any central test dataset. FedNIA injects random noise inputs to analyze the layerwise activation patterns in client models leveraging an autoencoder that detects abnormal behaviors indicative of data poisoning. FedNIA can defend against diverse attack types, including sample poisoning, label flipping, and backdoors, even in scenarios with multiple attacking nodes. Experimental results on non-iid federated datasets demonstrate its effectiveness and robustness, underscoring its potential as a foundational approach for enhancing the security of federated learning systems.
10.1109/tkde.2026.3736499: Federated Multi-Modal Recommender systems (FedMMRec) extend conventional federated recommendation frameworks by incorporating multi-modal content to boost model performance. However, current FedMMRec methods overlook two key issues.Firstly, due to the federated setting where each client observes only a subset of items, the server ends up with partial aggregated item representations, limiting its ability to model multi-modal embeddings.Secondly, at the client-side, multi-modal integration suffers from both data noise amplification and unresolved optimization conflicts across modalities. To tackle these issues, we propose Federated Multi-modal Recommendation with Structural Guidance and Robust Integration, namedFedMMSR.FedMMSRconsists of two modules, i.e., server-side Multi-modal Structural Guidance (MSG) and client-side Adaptive Robust Modality Integration (ARI). MSG constructs latent item-item graphs from multi-modal content to capture global structural relationships, thereby generating enriched multi-modal representations with higher-order semantics. In ARI, each client combines multi-modal noise-resistant loss with a personalized conflict-aware optimization mechanism. ARI aims to enhance noise resistance and adaptively resolve inter-modal conflict, achieving personalized modality balancing. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate the superior effectiveness ofFedMMSRin federated recommendation.
10.1109/tpds.2026.3735216: In this paper, we introduce FLEX, a flexible federated learning (FL) scheme that combines peer-to-peer communication with asynchronous client updates, enabling clients to operate independently. We further propose a novel aggregation algorithm inspired by gradient-like updates, governed by two key parameters: (i) a similarity-based aggregation weight to better handle non-IID data distributions, and (ii) a progress-based aggregation weight to mitigate straggler effects. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, FE-MNIST, and Boston Housing Dataset demonstrate that our aggregation algorithm achieves accuracy improvements of up to 13% over simple averaging (Avg) and 10% over FedProx under both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings, as well as IID and non-IID data distributions. Beyond aggregation, the FLEX scheme substantially outperforms state-of-the-art asynchronous centralized schemes (TimelyFL, FedBuff), delivering over 16% higher accuracy while reducing communication costs by factors of 10.4 and 13.6, respectively, for the same target accuracy. Compared to synchronous peer-to-peer approaches (Epidemic), FLEX reduces total training time by 2–$3\times$and communication by 40–50%. Compared to asynchronous P2P baselines (AsyDFL), FLEX reaches target accuracy levels$4\times$–$7.2\times$faster while reducing the number of exchanged updates by 50%–71%. Finally, relative to traditional synchronous centralized FedAvg, FLEX achieves accuracy gains of up to 23%.
10.1109/tac.2026.3733955: Scalable decentralized optimization in large-scale systems hinges on efficient communication. A common way to reduce communication overhead is to perform multiple local updates between two communication rounds, as in federated learning. However, extending this strategy to fully decentralized settings poses fundamental challenges. Existing decentralized algorithms with multiple local updates guarantee accurate convergence only under strong convexity, limiting applicability to the nonconvex problems prevalent in machine learning. Moreover, many methods require exchanging and storing auxiliary variables, such as gradient-tracking vectors or correction terms, to ensure convergence under data heterogeneity, incurring high communication and memory costs. In this paper, we propose MILE, a fully decentralized algorithm that guarantees both consensus and optimality under multiple local updates in general nonconvex settings. This is achieved through a novel periodic-system-based formulation and a lifting-based analysis, which together yield a closed-form expression for the state evolution across local updates, a theoretical advance not achieved previously. This closed-form characterization allows us to establish, for the first time, guaranteed consensus and optimality in decentralized nonconvex optimization under multiple local updates, in contrast to prior results that only ensure optimality of the average state. We prove that MILE achieves an $O(1/T)$ convergence rate under both exact and stochastic gradients, while requiring only a single variable exchange per interacting agent pair, minimizing communication and memory costs. Numerical experiments on benchmark datasets confirm its effectiveness.
10.1109/tpami.2026.3735649: In this paper, we introduce Hidden Subset Sum Problem (HSSP), a problem rooted in computational complexity and cryptographic applications, as a rigorous mathematical framework for analyzing privacy vulnerabilities in federated learning (FL). By applying HSSP to FL, this work addresses the limitations of gradient inversion attacks (GIA) by overcoming key challenges such as dependence on label diversity and poor performance with large batch sizes, which hinder existing empirical GIA methods. Additionally, our analysis uncovers the fundamental reasons behind the degradation of empirical GIA with increasing batch sizes. We further demonstrate that employing secure data aggregation techniques, such as secure multiparty computation, can significantly increase the attack's time complexity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to establish the connection between HSSP and FL, providing a robust analytical foundation for developing defense strategies and guiding future research.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3736712: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without sharing raw client data, but exchanged model updates may still leak sensitive information through gradient inversion (GI) attacks. Existing defenses often rely on gradient perturbation, cryptographic protocols, or architectural bottlenecks, which may introduce utility loss or additional system assumptions. In this work, we study empirical GI robustness in personalized federated learning from the perspective of representation divergence. We observe that personalized models can increase client-level latent misalignment, thereby making DLG/iDLG-style gradient matching less well-conditioned. Based on this insight, we propose Meta-PFL, a personalized FL framework that combines client-private VAE encoders, classifier-side model sharing, group-level meta-adaptation, and inter-group knowledge distillation. Under our threat model, the server or an external eavesdropper can observe uploaded classifier-side updates and knows the training protocol and model split, but cannot access raw data, client-private encoder parameters, encoder-side gradients, or stochastic latent samples. Meta-PFL does not provide formal differential privacy or cryptographic guarantees; instead, it aims to reduce reconstruction quality under the specified GI threat model while preserving utility under non-IID data. Experiments on Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 show that Meta-PFL achieves competitive or superior personalized accuracy and consistently reduces reconstruction quality under DLG/iDLG-style attacks. Additional evaluations with recent personalized FL baselines, stronger-budget GI stress tests, representation-divergence quantification, clustering-quality analysis, and efficiency measurements further support the effectiveness of the proposed framework.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3734103: This paper presents an asynchronous federated learning framework tailored for inertial measurement unit (IMU) systems. Traditional federated learning methods face substantial challenges when applied to the heterogeneous and time-sensitive characteristics of IMU data collected from wearable and mobile devices. The proposed framework introduces an adaptive asynchronous update mechanism that accounts for device-specific constraints while preserving model performance and convergence guarantees. Extensive experiments on publicly available motion-sensing datasets demonstrate that the method achieves faster convergence and higher macro-F1 than synchronous baselines, with reduced communication overhead. The approach proves particularly effective in human activity recognition and motion analysis applications, where IMU data often exhibit variability in sampling rates, signal quality, and availability. Moreover, the framework maintains robust performance under device heterogeneity and constrained communication budgets, sustaining competitive macro-F1 even under aggressive update compression.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3734977: Wireless Body Area Networks (WBANs) for remote health monitoring generate delay-sensitive patient data that requires low-latency processing. However, the limited computational resources of WBAN devices make local data processing challenging. Fog computing addresses this resource limitation problem by enabling data processing closer to patients. However, the limited resources of Fog Servers (FSs) require efficient allocation to reduce latency and energy consumption. Moreover, health data analysis requires accurate processing with minimal loss. Therefore, to address these challenges, this paper formulates a cost-minimization problem keeping latency, energy, and loss function in deliberation. To solve the formulated problem, Cost Minimization Algorithm (CMA) has been proposed using Follow The Perturbed Leader (FTPL) supporting Federated Learning (FL)-based Federated Averaging (FedAvg) technique. The FTPL technique is utilized to select efficient FS, and FedAvg performs processing of WBAN data accurately with minimized loss function value. Through experimental and prototype demonstrations, the efficacy of proposed CMA framework is shown by achieving a 40.05% reduction in the average total cost compared to other State-of-the-Art (SOTA) technique on a real-world data set.
10.1109/tccn.2026.3734985: Federated learning (FL) has become a promising paradigm for privacy-preserving and communication-efficient model training in vehicular networks. With the continuous expansion of vehicular networks, multiple FL tasks are often initiated concurrently by moving vehicles, which poses substantial challenges to the conventional single-task FL framework that relies on round-robin execution. Thus, effective vehicle scheduling is required to support concurrent participation in multiple FL tasks. Moreover, the straggler effect caused by vehicle heterogeneity can lead to inefficient resource utilization, as faster-training vehicles remain idle while waiting for slower ones. To address these challenges, we propose a distributed multi-task FL framework that enables independent and parallel execution of multiple FL tasks. A delay-driven hierarchical vehicle scheduling strategy is developed, which preferentially assigns vehicles with stronger training capabilities to tasks with more stringent latency requirements. To balance training latency and accuracy, we design a dynamic accuracy function, based on which a task utility function is defined. Subject to vehicle waiting-time constraints, we formulate a joint optimization problem that determines the number of global training rounds for each task, uplink bandwidth allocation, and vehicle CPU frequency to maximize the overall system utility. To solve it, we design a novel multi-agent twin-delayed deep deterministic policy gradient (MATD3)-based round-aware and resource optimization algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme significantly improves system utility while reducing total energy consumption compared with baseline methods.
10.1109/tce.2026.3735776: Collaborative learning systems in resource-limited edge networks provide a privacy-preserving paradigm; however, regulations such as the “Right to be Forgotten” require Federated Unlearning (FU) to remove the influence of specific data. Existing FU research primarily focuses on efficiency, while security risks during distributed unlearning–particularly the performance recovery phase–remain less examined. Conventional backdoor attacks often rely on static triggers that may be weakened by unlearning. We propose LURA, a dynamic attack framework that exploits the unlearning-recovery procedure to reintroduce persistent backdoor behavior. Rather than resisting unlearning, the adversary requests removal to trigger recovery. LURA uses a Shadow Dataset to construct a Dynamic Legitimate Template that estimates locally acceptable update characteristics without a global view. It further uses a Cancellation Gradient that combines a recovery-aligned component with a dormant malicious component. This design enables the backdoor to be reactivated during recovery under the evaluated threat model. Across the four dataset/model settings in Table I, after unlearning and the specified 14-round recovery procedure, LURA improves post-unlearning attack success rate (P-ASR) by 42.26 percentage points and main-task accuracy (ACC) by 0.51 percentage points, on average, over the best listed static-backdoor baseline for each metric. Gradient Stealthiness Score (GSS) is used as a relative update-alignment measure. These findings suggest that FU security should consider both deletion and subsequent recovery stages.
10.1109/tce.2026.3735750: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across networked clients without centralizing raw data, yet faces challenges in server-side communication load and statistical heterogeneity. As FL deployments scale to hundreds or thousands of clients, the central-server uplink becomes a critical bottleneck while non-IID data distributions degrade convergence. This paper presents FedCluster, a hierarchical federated learning framework addressing these challenges through three coordinated mechanisms: (i) gradient-signature-based dynamic clustering that groups clients by training behavior, (ii) a Proxy Validation Unit (PVU) that filters biased or adversarial updates using fairness-aware weighting, and (iii) a two-level aggregation scheme reducingcentral-server uplinkcommunication fromO(Nd)toO(Kd)per round. Unlike existing clustered FL methods relying on static partitioning, FedCluster adapts client-cluster assignments dynamically based on training signatures. On the supervised CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 experiments under severe non-IID conditions (Dirichletα= 0.1), FedCluster improves accuracy by approximately 6 percentage points over FedAvg with stable convergence; the ablation attributes this gain jointly to an enhanced cluster-specific architecture and to dynamic clustering. On the HAR and MHEALTH activity benchmarks, evaluated separately as unsupervised federated clustering with simulated clients, the label-free variant FedCluster–U attains the highest ARI on MHEALTH and is competitive on HAR; these clustering results are not part of the +6-point claim. The server-uplink reduction is not an end-to-end saving: total communication is about 1.2× that of FedAvg, training time is 67% longer, and peak memory is 1.8×, an overhead that is justified when the server link, rather than client bandwidth or device resources, is the binding constraint. These results validate that hierarchical restructuring with fairness-aware validation provides a practical path toward robust federated learning with substantially reduced server-side communication.
10.1109/taes.2026.3733921: The evolution of low Earth orbit satellite constellations demands artificial intelligence (AI) frameworks that reconcile decentralized intelligence with extreme energy constraints. This article presents AstraFL—a federated learning paradigm for orbital edge computing that fundamentally rethinks model coordination through three conceptual innovations. First, we introduce a hybrid consensus architecture merging gossip-based peer-to-peer synchronization with blockchain-secured validation, enabling autonomous model aggregation across dynamic intersatellite networks without ground station dependencies. This dual-layer coordination mechanism establishes trust through probabilistically verified transactions while maintaining sublinear communication scaling. Second, we develop dynamic Block Minifloat arithmetic with hardware-algorithmic co-design, implementing adaptive precision scaling that automatically optimizes bit-width allocation across model training phases. This approach fundamentally rebalances the energy–accuracy trade space through layerwise quantization sensitivity analysis and radiation-hardened field programmable gate array (FPGA) acceleration. Third, the framework pioneers task-parallel federated updates through decomposed aggregation primitives, enabling simultaneous intraplane model merging and cross-plane gradient validation. Experimental validation across orbital hardware testbeds demonstrates how these architectural innovations collectively resolve the decentralization–security–efficiency trilemma: maintaining 98.7% model fidelity with 3.5× energy reduction versus FP32 baselines while achieving Byzantine fault tolerance through our stochastic proof-of-stake protocol. By redefining the coordination mechanisms and numerical foundations of spaceborne AI, AstraFL establishes an improved paradigm for autonomous learning in next-generation satellite constellations.
10.1109/ton.2026.3734988: To alleviate the training burden in federated learning while enhancing convergence speed, Split Federated Learning (SFL) has emerged as a promising approach by combining the advantages of federated and split learning. However, despite its advantages, existing SFL studies have largely overlooked the strategic interactions among self-interested participants during the SFL process. In this framework, the SFL model owner can choose the cut layer to balance the training load between the server and clients, ensuring the necessary level of privacy for the clients. Additionally, the SFL model owner sets incentives to encourage client participation in the SFL process.
