The optimization strategies employed by the SFL model owner influence clients' decisions regarding the amount of data they contribute, taking into account the shared incentives over clients and anticipated energy consumption from both computation and networking during SFL. To address this framework, we model the problem using a hierarchical decision-making approach, formulated as a single-leader multi-follower Stackelberg game. We demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of the Nash equilibrium among clients and analyze the Stackelberg equilibrium by examining the leader's game. Furthermore, we discuss privacy concerns related to differential privacy and the criteria for selecting the minimum required cut layer. Our findings show that the Stackelberg equilibrium solution maximizes the utility for both the clients and the SFL model owner while achieving a well-balanced trade-off between model accuracy and the associated computing and networking overhead during the SFL process.
10.1109/tnnls.2026.3732298: Cross-domain federated learning (CFL) suffers from degraded generalization due to feature discrepancies across clients. Most existing methods improve generalization by aligning cross-domain semantic features or enhancing feature diversity. However, they lack explicit constraints on the structural consistency of feature spaces and fail to distinguish semantic consistency from structural alignment. To address this, we propose FedDSSA, a novel framework that explicitly decouples structural alignment and semantic alignment in CFL. For structural alignment, we introduce a globally shared prototype classifier and enforce a uniform feature distribution in the latent space, ensuring consistent geometric structures of class representations across clients. For semantic alignment, FedDSSA generates virtual domain features to guide local representations toward a globally consistent semantic space, thereby reducing cross-domain discrepancies. Furthermore, we validate the effectiveness and underlying mechanisms of FedDSSA through representation quantification metrics. Extensive experiments on five benchmark datasets demonstrate that FedDSSA improves generalization performance by an average of 2.90% and enhances personalization by 4.96%, effectively boosting cross-domain generalization capability.
10.1109/tifs.2026.3734781: To remove the contribution of specific data from the global model in federated learning, federated unlearning has recently emerged. Existing approaches face challenges such as reliance on full client participation, the need to store historical model updates, and high communication costs. To overcome these limitations, we propose Practical Federated Unlearning (PFU), a target client-driven approach to model forgetting with only a single round of interaction between the target client and the aggregation server during the unlearning stage. To fulfill PFU, the aggregation server utilizes the Fisher Information Matrix to identify the most sensitive parameters with respect to the target client’s data and sends their indices to the target client. Then, the target client estimates its contribution to the sensitive parameters using a Bayesian inference-based method, thus avoiding the requirement for data or historical model updates from all other clients. Finally, it prunes the sensitive parameters with a tailored mechanism, which achieves effective unlearning of the data knowledge while preventing catastrophic forgetting. Theoretical analysis under explicit regularity assumptions and experimental results confirm the effectiveness and practical advantages of PFU.
10.1109/twc.2026.3737404: Federated Learning (FL) is a promising technique for privacy-preserving edge machine learning. However, it suffers from heavy communication overhead caused by massive edge devices and poor interpretability incurred by closed box deep neural networks. In this paper, we, for the first time, study the statistical optimality of the gradient descent (GD) algorithm in an over-the-air computation (AirComp)-based FL system with shallow neural networks (ShaNNs). Specifically, we propose an AirComp-based FL system that uses polynomial ShaNNs as machine learning models for statistical analysis on edge devices. However, the aggregated gradient is corrupted by the receiver noise of AirComp. To tackle this challenge, we prove that the Frobenius norm of the noise matrix can be bounded if the signal-to-noise ratio and the number of devices are large enough. With this bound, in the first several iterations, the GD trajectory will iterate towards the ground-truth point. We also theoretically characterize the estimation gap between the iteration point and the ground-truth point. In particular, the GD trajectory will stop iterating towards the ground-truth point after some global iterations due to the corruption of noise. Numerical results show that our proposed method enjoys a similar success rate to the noise-free scheme and also verify the proposed theoretical analysis.
10.1109/ton.2026.3734385: Over-the-air federated learning (OTA-FL) offers an exciting advancement over classical FL using the physics of analog signal propagation for model update aggregation. Since each participant broadcasts its model weights concurrently in time and frequency, this paradigm conserves communication bandwidth and model upload latency. Despite its potential, no prior large-scale real-world demonstration exists. This paper is the first to demonstrate OTA-FL deployment in a cellular network within the constraints of a 5G-compliant OFDM (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing) waveform. We identify key challenges, including multi-path fading, thermal noise, and the need for precise client synchronization for coherent OTA aggregation. To address these, we propose a unified real-world implementation incorporating pre-equalization, model update-to-OFDM mapping, and a dual-layer synchronization interface for OTA-FL training. Additionally, we develop a simulation framework in NVIDIA Sionna for large-scale evaluations in an urban microcell (UMi) environment, integrating an adaptive power control scheme to manage complex outdoor propagation. We experimentally validate OTA-FL for Channel Estimation and Object Classification using the ORBIT testbed with users at varying distances, along with an indoor testbed featuring a mobile client for dynamic channel conditions. Furthermore, we analyze model generalization and adaptive power control across a wide-range emulated urban cell, along with additional operator-level benefits. Under specific conditions, OTA-FL achieves comparable model performance while improving spectrum utilization by$43\times $and energy efficiency by$7\times $over classical FL with five participants, with the benefits growing proportionally as more participants are added.
10.1109/tifs.2026.3734774: Federated Learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving distributed model training, but it is still vulnerable to model poisoning attacks that can degrade global performance or introduce backdoors. Existing defense methods often rely on single-band features or strong assumptions, which limit their robustness and scalability under non-IID settings. This paper presents DualFreqFL, a frequency-decoupled dual-server framework designed for robust and communication-efficient federated learning. By leveraging a two-level discrete wavelet transform, DualFreqFL decomposes client updates into low- and high-frequency components. These components are transmitted to two separate servers: the detection server conducts clustering-based consistency analysis on low-frequency features to identify potential anomalies, while the aggregation server handles sparse, high-frequency components for secure and efficient global model reconstruction. A dynamic retransmission mechanism ensures complete anomaly verification without redundant communication. Security analysis demonstrates that DualFreqFL not only prevents any single server from recovering complete updates but also maintains robustness and fairness even under high attacker ratios and long-term training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DualFreqFL outperforms existing methods in robustness, communication efficiency, and security. Compared to full model transmission, it reduces communication cost by more than 59% while ensuring complete anomaly verification. Moreover, it achieves 100% malicious client detection accuracy under the evaluated non-adaptive poisoning attacks while maintaining robust performance under non-IID data distributions.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3737601: Federated learning distributes data among $n$ clients, making it vulnerable to malicious attacks and data heterogeneity, which together pose challenges for robust learning. To tackle this issue, centered clipping and Huber aggregators have been exploited for Byzantine robustness. In this paper, we first demonstrate their equivalence via convex conjugate theory, and show that they can yield biased solutions in the presence of outliers, leading to failure under high data heterogeneity and a substantial fraction of outliers. Next, we propose a new robust aggregation rule that utilizes the truncated-quadratic (TQ) loss, effectively mitigating the biases of existing methods, such as centered clipping and Huber aggregators. We show that our aggregator achieves order-optimal Byzantine-robust learning under nonconvex loss functions and heterogeneous data, ultimately enhancing the reliability of federated learning systems. Additionally, we provide a robust deviation estimation strategy for TQ, demonstrating its effectiveness. Furthermore, we show that TQ maintains robustness even when only an estimate of the number of Byzantine clients is available. Finally, experimental results on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, indicate that our aggregator provides better robustness performance than the competing techniques.
10.1109/tpds.2026.3733289: Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) enables clients to collaboratively train personalized models tailored to their individual objectives, addressing the challenge of model generalization in traditional Federated Learning (FL) due to high data heterogeneity. However, existing PFL methods often require increased communication rounds to achieve the desired performance, primarily due to slow training caused by the use of first-order optimization, which has linear convergence. Additionally, many of these methods increase local computation because of the additional data fed into the model during the search for personalized local models. One promising solution to this slow training is second-order optimization, known for its quadratic convergence. However, employing it in PFL is challenging due to the Hessian matrix and its inverse. In this paper, we propose pFedSOP, which efficiently utilizes second-order optimization in PFL to accelerate the training of personalized models and enhance performance with fewer communication rounds. Our approach first computes a personalized local gradient update using the Gompertz function-based normalized angle between local and global gradient updates, incorporating client-specific global information. We then use a regularized Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), computed from this personalized gradient update, as an approximation of the Hessian to update the personalized models. This FIM-based second-order optimization speeds up training with fewer communication rounds by tackling the challenges with exact Hessian and avoids additional data being fed into the model during the search for personalized local models. Extensive experiments on heterogeneously partitioned image classification datasets with partial client participation demonstrate that pFedSOP outperforms state-of-the-art FL and PFL algorithms.
10.1109/tmm.2026.3736516: While current federated multimodal continual learning over mixture-of-experts low-rank adaptation (MoE-LoRA) is built on the unverified assumption that routing isolates task-specific knowledge into disjoint experts, we argue that routing operates per-sample, while forgetting accumulates across the task sequence, and gradient conflict persists within each expert even when routing is maximally polarized. Moreover, activation-subspace protection can also fail because, under parameter-efficient fine-tuning, it entangles tasks due to a dimension-counting bound, and federated averaging (FedAvg) disrupts client-side orthogonality. To address this, we propose POLARIS (Per-expertOrthogonalLandscape-AwareRouting-InformedSubspace protection), which maintains a per-expert protection basis in the gradient subspace, preserves its orthogonality under FedAvg with a bounded truncation loss at each basis union, and reinterprets MoE routing as a capacity allocator. Our results show that, on LLaVA-1.5-7B, LLaVA-1.5-13B, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B across CoIN-6 and CoIN-Long-10, POLARIS outperforms fourteen state-of-the-art baselines in average accuracy. Compared to the best federated multimodal baseline, the performance margin increases from$+3.16$pp on CoIN-6 to$+6.00$pp on CoIN-Long-10.
10.1109/tsp.2026.3737023: We propose PRISM-FCP (Partial shaRing and robust calIbration with Statistical Margins for Federated Conformal Prediction), a communication-efficient Byzantine-robust federated conformal prediction framework that uses partial model sharing to mitigate stochastic model-poisoning attacks during training and histogram-based filtering to mitigate adversarial calibration submissions. Existing robust FCP approaches primarily address adversarial behavior during calibration, leaving training-stage poisoning to separate robust-training mechanisms. PRISM-FCP instead considers the coupling between the two stages. During training, clients partially share updates by transmitting only $M$ of $D$ parameters per round. Under the stated stochastic attack model, this attenuates the expected energy of each Byzantine client's perturbation contribution to the aggregate by a factor of $M/D$ relative to full sharing. When this benefit outweighs the optimization slowdown caused by partial updates, it can reduce training error and improve interval efficiency. During calibration, the server uses client-provided characterization vectors to filter suspected Byzantine clients before estimating the conformal quantile from the retained clients. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and the UCI Superconductivity and YearPredictionMSD datasets, including Gaussian, ALIE, and sign-flipping training-stage attacks, demonstrate near-nominal empirical coverage and favorable communication--performance tradeoffs in the studied settings.
10.1109/tccn.2026.3735680: Wireless Federated Learning (FL) enables User Equipments (UEs) to collaboratively train a shared model under the coordination of the Base Station (BS) without exposing their private data. However, due to limited computation and communication resources, some UEs may be unable to train the full model, causing the global model to miss important data features and resulting in degraded performance. Even when training is possible, UEs often cannot complete each round at the same pace, leading to the synchronization barrier and increased overall time. In this paper, we propose FedPB, a framework that accelerates wireless FL by dynamically adjusting the pruning ratios and bandwidth allocation. Specifically, we formulate a joint pruning ratio and bandwidth allocation optimization problem that minimizes the total completion time under resource constraints while ensuring convergence. We theoretically analyze the convergence behavior, and based on the analysis, decompose the joint optimization problem into subproblems, which are solved iteratively. Extensive experiments on both CNN-based vision tasks and Transformer-based language tasks demonstrate that FedPB achieves up to 5× speedup under resource constraints while preserving the performance of the global model.
10.1109/tvt.2026.3735840: Paging is a fundamental service in mobile communication networks that enables the network to locate idle user equipment (UE) when downlink data arrives. In emerging 6G networks, the traditional paging mechanism lacks intelligence and faces significant challenges in handling the massive number of mobile terminal accesses, resulting in substantial signaling resource overhead. Moreover, existing paging systems lack effective privacy-preserving capabilities, thereby posing potential privacy risks when user mobility data is used for intelligent analytics. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a Privacy-Preserving and Intelligent Paging System (FL-DPIP). In the proposed framework, a Transformer-based signaling data processing method, namely Trs-PRE, is introduced to capture temporal and spatial patterns in UE mobility data and improve the accuracy of user location prediction. Furthermore, we design a privacy-enhanced architecture that integrates Federated Learning (FL) and Differential Privacy (DP) within a distributed NWDAF framework, enabling collaborative model training without sharing raw user data while mitigating potential privacy leakage. Experimental results demonstrate that FL-DPIP reduces signaling resource consumption by 67% compared with the traditional paging system. In addition, the privacy capability analysis shows that FL-DPIP enables intelligent paging while providing effective privacy protection, making it one of the first intelligent paging systems with built-in privacy-preserving capability for 6G networks.
10.1109/tsc.2026.3735705: Cross-institutional federated learning can be delivered as a service in which institution-operated clients return local model updates to a coordination service. Non-identically distributed (Non-IID) clinical data and poisoned contributions complicate reliable composition, while communication and latency constrain operation. We present AGRA, an anchor-guided reputation-aware policy that radius-normalizes contributions, measures disagreement against a momentum anchor, and converts cross-round reputation into support decisions and composition weights after a robust warm-up. On PathMNIST with 20 service entities and a 30% malicious-entity ratio, AGRA reaches final validation accuracies of 86.38%, 85.11%, and 84.82% under label flipping, sign flipping, and low-amplitude anti-mean poisoning, exceeding the strongest competing final result by 1.70, 1.16, and 1.45 percentage points. Its 87.13% clean accuracy trails FoundationFL-m1's 90.24%, exposing a functional-QoS trade-off. An optional single-workstation score-execution service adds 5.9% mean latency and 13.5% accounted logical-payload communication over FedAvg; it characterizes operational cost, not confidentiality against the authorized coordinator. Evidence is limited to one dataset, full participation, and exact full-dimensional utility scoring.
10.1109/tce.2026.3735576: The rapid evolution of women-centric consumer electronics has promoted the adoption of federated learning (FL) for privacy-preserving health monitoring over distributed user data. In real-world deployments, clients often require heterogeneous private model architectures tailored to different sensing modalities, device capabilities, and application-specific health tasks. HFL addresses model heterogeneity by enabling proxy-based knowledge sharing, but existing frameworks still lack efficient zero-knowledge verification of submitted updates and auditable admission control for trusted cross-device and cross-institution collaboration. We therefore propose BVPHFL: A Blockchain-Assisted Verifiable and Privacy-Preserving Heterogeneous Federated Learning Framework for Women-Centric Consumer Electronics. In BVPHFL, each client locally trains a private model and a proxy model through a prescribed private–proxy learning process, and submits only the resulting proxy update for global collaboration. Zero-knowledge proofs verify the provenance of submitted proxy updates and their correspondence to the training round, and certify the correctness of aggregation over the admitted update set, while preserving the confidentiality of raw data and private training states against the coordinator, verifier contract, and other participants. The blockchain provides an auditable record of admitted updates before global aggregation. Experiments on benchmark screening workloads show comparable utility in most evaluated tasks and characterize the efficiency of update validation and aggregation.
10.1109/tccn.2026.3735674: Personalized Federated Learning (PFL) addresses performance degradation in non-IID settings by preserving personalized local models. However, the inherent reinitialization of local models in each communication round weakens cross-client knowledge transfer, which disrupts the balance between global and local knowledge. This imbalance restricts the utilization of shared representations, resulting in biased feature extraction that ultimately limits the model’s personalization performance. To solve this problem, we propose Feature Distribution Alignment (FDA), a general FL framework that enhances collaborative knowledge transfer. It consists of two components, namely Consensus Knowledge Guidance (CKG) and Local Knowledge Memory (LKM). CKG employs a domain adversarial approach adapted to FL settings, guiding local feature extractors toward globally consistent representations. LKM retains historical local features via attention-based fusion and mutual information maximization, enhancing feature alignment while reducing redundancy. This combined mechanism ensures the persistent retention of prior knowledge in local models despite continuous global model updates. By integrating these components, the FDA enables local feature extractors to better align with global knowledge while maintaining personalization. This design effectively balances global and local knowledge while improving local model performance. Theoretical analysis provides generalization guarantees supporting the effectiveness of FDA in facilitating server-to-client knowledge transfer. Extensive experiments on four datasets under three statistically heterogeneous settings show that FedAvg+FDA outperforms leading PFL methods in terms of effectiveness, stability, and fairness. Our code is available athttps://github.com/NiantaoZ/FedFDA.
10.1109/tpami.2026.3736784: Adapting large pretrained foundation models (PFMs) to private domains presents significant challenges related to data privacy and limited client resources. In this study, we delve into large PFMs adaptation in the resource-constrained federated learning environment, and propose an innovative framework, which alternates between large model distillation and resource-adaptive pruning, with guaranteed convergence. Our framework, namely ADRAP, confers a dual advantage. First, the alternating pipeline balances retaining intrinsic PFMs capabilities with assimilating new domain knowledge from local private data. Additionally, our novel distilling-while-adaptive-pruning strategy dynamically accommodates heterogeneous client resources, ensuring effective collaborative optimization under arbitrary constraints. Theoretically, we establish upper bounds for parameter updates during both the distillation and pruning-based adaptation stages and further demonstrate that ADRAP maintains an asymptotically optimal convergence rate $O(1/\sqrt{\rho TQ})$. Empirical results reveal that ADRAP outperforms state-of-the-art baselines by up to 14.23% (at $a=0.1$) for NLP tasks and 20.55% (under IID) for CV tasks in average accuracy across both domains, demonstrating its effectiveness and adaptability in federated large model adaptation.
10.1109/tcc.2026.3735701: Federated learning keeps raw data on local devices, but wireless deployments still suffer from substantial communication energy consumption, hierarchy-induced delay, and privacy risks caused by heterogeneous channel conditions. This paper studies a nested federated multi-task architecture with one macro edge server, multiple micro edge servers (mESs), and heterogeneous end clients that maintain both a general task model and a lightweight resource allocation optimization (RAO) model. The RAO model uses round-wise channel and device states to determine subcarrier and power allocation, while the task model performs application-level learning under the allocated communication budget. We reformulate the joint subcarrier and power allocation problem as a constrained energy-minimization problem with explicit rate, power, and assignment constraints, and we further clarify the dual-model computation overhead, the latency impact of the two-level hierarchy, and the scope of privacy computing as FL-based data locality rather than a formal privacy guarantee. To better capture time-varying wireless conditions, the adopted channel model combines Okumura-Hata large-scale path loss with round-wise block fading. Simulation results in medium-scale scenarios show that the proposed nested strategy achieves favorable communication-energy performance and run-to-run stability compared with the implemented heuristic and learning-based baselines, while clarifying the operating assumptions and limitations of the framework.
10.1109/tkde.2026.3736816: Recent privacy regulations increasingly emphasize the right to erase the impact of individual participants in Federated Learning (FL), a distributed learning paradigm in which multiple clients collaboratively train a global model without sharing their local data. Existing approaches tackle this Federated Unlearning (FU) problem primarily by partitioning client data into disjoint shards, thereby confining the impact of revoked clients. However, the fundamental challenges of FL, such as non-IID data distributions and stochastic participation during training, remain significant obstacles to achieving both efficient and effective FU. To overcome these limitations, this paper presents a novel adaptive data partitioning framework. We first establish inter-shard relationships via a personalized aggregation mechanism, which significantly alleviates the model accuracy degradation caused by disjoint sharding and non-IID data, while still ensuring confined unlearning overhead. Additionally, we propose a dynamic client-to-shard reassignment strategy. It accelerates FU by balancing the distribution of unlearning workloads, especially when processing successive revocations. Furthermore, clients within each shard are partitioned into fine-grained slices, enabling prioritized participation scheduling and adaptive slice sizing to enhance overall performance. Evaluations conducted in both simulated and real-world FL scenarios demonstrate that our framework runs 4× faster with an improvement of 6× in accuracy, compared to state-of-the-art competitors.
10.1109/tpami.2026.3736862: Auction-based Federated Learning (AFL) provides a principled framework for incentivizing self-interested data owners (DOs) to participate in collaborative learning initiated by data consumers (DCs) through market mechanisms. A central challenge in AFL is to determine how a budget-constrained DC should bid for data-use rights. Existing methods often conflate the submitted bid with the realized payment. This treatment is inconsistent with the widely adopted second-price sealed-bid (SPSB) mechanism, in which the highest bidder wins but pays the market price determined by the competing bids rather than its own bid. Moreover, the market price is observed by a target DC only after a win; after a loss, the DC observes only that the market price exceeds its submitted bid, producing right-censored feedback. To address these challenges, we propose KMM-AFL, a return-on-investment (ROI)-aware bidding framework that explicitly separates bid price from expected SPSB payment and combines DO utility estimation with request-conditioned market-price modeling. KMM-AFL uses a conditional Kaplan Meier (KM) construction to exploit both winning and losing auction records. Because exact repetitions of high-dimensional bid requests are sparse, a conditional Markov Network estimates the observed winning-price and losing-probability terms required by KM. The recovered request-conditioned market-price distribution and the estimated DO valuation are then used to select the largest bid satisfying a common expected-return requirement and the remaining-budget constraint. Extensive evaluations across 6 benchmark datasets show that KMM-AFL outperforms state-of the-art baselines, achieving a 16.56% increase in DC utility and a 3.36% improvement in FL model accuracy.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3736717: Federated edge learning (FEEL) has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for achieving edge intelligence (EI) via enabling collaborative model training across edge devices while protecting data privacy. In this paper, we put forth an online optimization framework that jointly manages federated training and inference on resource-constrained edge devices. We introduce a tandem-queue-inspired conversion mechanism that bridges inference requests and training data, and further incorporate both data and model freshness into the accuracy formulation to capture temporal dynamics in real-world environments. To maximize inference accuracy while minimizing latency and energy consumption, the mode selections, communication, and computation resource allocations of edge devices are jointly optimized. We formulate this optimization as a multi-objective optimization problem, which is NP-hard and further complicated by the online setting. To address these challenges, we transform the problem into a multi-objective Markov decision process (MOMDP) and develop a \underline{c}onstrained \underline{m}ulti-\underline{o}bjective \underline{p}roximal \underline{p}olicy \underline{o}ptimization (C-MOPPO) algorithm. Specifically, C-MOPPO first learns a set of policies with different preferences across three objectives, then leverages constrained policy optimization to enrich the Pareto front and obtain high-quality, dense solutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that C-MOPPO achieves well-balanced trade-offs among objectives and significantly outperforms baselines under various system configurations.
10.1109/tr.2026.3736807: Federated Learning (FL) is increasingly adopted in distributed and privacy-preserving applications for decentralized intelligence, yet it remains highly vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Existing defenses remain fundamentally limited to single-attack scenarios, which overlook the real-world risk of coordinated, multi-vector attacks. This work presents a comprehensive framework for composite attack in FL, where adversaries simultaneously deploy label flipping, feature manipulation, and data poisoning across clients. We formalize the concept of composite attacks and prove that their joint effect is non-additive, governed by a quadratic interaction structure in gradient space, producing amplification effects. We define and formalize the attack interaction and amplification phenomenon, where multiple attacks spontaneously align in gradient space, causing greater damage than individual attacks. Under the non convex optimization setting, we theoretically demonstrate that composite attacks cause optimization instability and increase gradient variance, while empirically exposing the vulnerability of several existing defenses on benchmark MNIST, CIFAR-100, and NSL-KDD datasets under single and composite attack scenarios. Additionally, we introduce the attack interaction score (AIS) and the attack amplification ratio (AAR) to quantify the interaction and amplification effect caused by the composite attack. These findings expose critical gaps in current FL defense strategies and underscore the urgent need for adaptive, composite-resilient solutions to secure FL systems against sophisticated adversaries.
10.1109/tcsvt.2026.3735054: Spectral clustering has emerged as one of the most effective clustering algorithms due to its superior performance. However, most existing models are designed for centralized settings, rendering them inapplicable in modern decentralized environments. Moreover, current federated learning approaches often suffer from poor generalization performance due to reliance on unreliable pseudo-labels, and fail to capture the latent correlations amongst heterogeneous clients. To tackle these limitations, this paper proposes a novel framework named Federated Multi-Task Clustering (i.e.,FMTC), which intends to learn personalized clustering models for heterogeneous clients while collaboratively leveraging their shared underlying structure in a privacy-preserving manner. More specifically, the FMTC framework is composed of two main components: client-side personalized clustering module, which learns a parameterized mapping model to support robust out-of-sample inference, bypassing the need for unreliable pseudo-labels; and server-side tensorial correlation module, which explicitly captures the shared knowledge across all clients. This is achieved by organizing all client models into a unified tensor and applying a low-rank regularization to discover their common subspace. To solve this joint optimization problem, we derive an efficient, privacy-preserving distributed algorithm based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, which decomposes the global problem into parallel local updates on clients and an aggregation step on the server. To the end, several extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed FMTC framework significantly outperforms various baseline and state-of-the-art federated clustering algorithms.
10.1109/tccn.2026.3734999: This paper studies a DT training problem in a resources-constrained edge network scenario. An Over-the-Air Computation assisted Bayesian Federated Meta-Learning (ABFM) framework is first proposed for DT training, which relieves the computing resources constrained problem in DT training by enabling a DT model with fast adaptation capability and relieves the bandwidth resources constrained problem in DT training by using an AirComp scheme for global aggregation. The convergence of the ABFM framework is derived to analyze the main factors that affect the upper bound of a global model’s convergence error. A novel AirComp scheme is proposed for DT training based on the ABFM framework to improve the transmission efficiency for DT training in the network. The DT training problem is formulated as a mixed integer programming problem with an objective to minimize a weighted sum of the convergence residuals of DT models, DT training delay, and the energy consumption of DT training by jointly optimizing the selection of user devices, the design of beamforming, and the allocation of CPU frequencies. An ABFM-based DT Training (ABFM-DTT) algorithm is proposed to solve the formulated problem. Simulation results show that the proposed ABFM framework and ABFM-DTT algorithm can achieve better performance than several benchmark frameworks and algorithms in terms of DT model accuracy, DT training delay and DT training energy consumption.
10.1109/tcss.2026.3733116: The rapid digitalization of education worldwide has made learning analytics (LA) a core part of modern educational infrastructure, increasing the need for robust artificial intelligence (AI) systems that can automatically infer students’ learning states and support reliable decisions. Federated learning (FL) enables geographically distributed institutions to jointly train affective recognition models while keeping raw institutional data local. At the same time, deploying FL in educational settings raises important security risks. The nonindependent and identically distributed nature of institution-level educational data and recording conditions can obscure compromised clients, enabling stealthy backdoors that hide indicators of distress or exaggerate engagement-related affective signals. These attacks reduce the trustworthiness of AI-assisted analytics and can distort downstream intervention decisions. To address these risks, we propose a proactive defense framework for federated affective analytics systems. Our method is motivated by the observation that backdoor attacks often exploit model capacity that is rarely used during normal training. Based on this idea, we introduce a server-side redundancy saturation mechanism that uses public out-of-distribution (OOD) data to occupy redundant parameter space, while using synthetic in-distribution (ID) proxy data to stabilize ID behavior and preserve performance on the primary emotion-recognition task. The proposed procedure does not require server access to raw client data and can be integrated into existing FL workflows. Experiments on public affect-recognition proxy benchmarks under diverse federated settings show that, across the main attack evaluations, our framework reduces the worst-case backdoor accuracy from 92.15% without defense to 10.19%, while preserving main-task accuracy, supporting its use as a security component for federated educational affective LA.
10.1109/tvt.2026.3735297: With the rapid development of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV), the explosive growth in data volume has raised concerns about data privacy. Federated Learning (FL), as a decentralized machine learning technology, can effectively protect data privacy. However, FL applications in IoV scenarios still face significant challenges, mainly reflected in the lack of fairness in incentive mechanism design and insufficient consideration of the impact of high vehicle mobility on the FL process. These issues can lead to insufficient vehicle participation, which limits the effectiveness of model training. To address these challenges in the dynamic environment of IoV, we propose a dynamic incentive mechanism based on the Stackelberg game. The mechanism aims to improve the fairness of the incentive mechanism by optimizing reward distribution and contribution evaluation, thereby promoting active vehicle participation and comprehensively considering the impact of vehicle mobility on the incentive process. Theoretical analysis and experimental results demonstrate that our scheme effectively enhances the fairness of the system and improves the performance of the global model.
10.1109/tii.2026.3726857: Decentralized federated learning (DFL) enables privacy-preserving training without a central server, removing the single-point-of-failure risk of centralized federated learning. In highly dynamic settings, such as the Internet of Vehicles (IoV), device heterogeneity causes stragglers, while time-varying links and no global coordination complicate load balancing and aggregation scheduling. Cooperation relieves stragglers but couples a node's training cost with its neighbors' resources, blurring individual contributions and complicating aggregation-node selection in dynamic networks. To address these challenges, we propose DMASFL, a decentralized multiagent split federated learning (SFL) framework for dynamic edge networks like IoV. DMASFL models each roadside unit (RSU) in the IoV as an autonomous, partially observable agent that self-organizes into clusters and decides participation, resource allocation, and SFL cooperation. Each cluster trains cooperatively and aggregates locally, and cluster heads gossip across clusters for final aggregation. DMASFL includes two mechanisms to optimize cooperation: dynamic adaptive head election elects heads by candidate-induced aggregation-path loss and historical service load, and active bottleneck-set credit assignment estimates key nodes' marginal effect on team utility via single-node counterfactual replacement, with residual correction for multinode interactions. On DroneVehicle, DMASFL outperforms representative mutliagent reinforcement learning and DFL baselines in throughput, training efficiency, and load balancing. Sensitivity, scalability, and MIMII-DUE validation show that DMASFL remains effective under stale information, varying RSU scales, and latency and communication constraints.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3734683: Deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) at the wireless edge is hampered by the “communication wall”: traditional Federated Learning (FL), an offline training paradigm, necessitates exchanging gigabyte-scale parameters, violating real-time latency constraints over fading channels and exposing gradient-based privacy vulnerabilities. For collaboration among already deployed models, we propose Communication-efficient Inference Token Exchange (CITE), a decentralized inference-time framework. CITE employs a lightweight semantic signaling protocol governed by a dual-sided Sanitization-Decomposition mechanism, which bounds sequence-level leakage of sensitive private attributes under explicit context-leakage assumptions. To mitigate the impact of unreliable peers in non-stationary wireless networks, we design a Synergistic Trust Consensus algorithm incorporating a Temperature-Scaled Weighting scheme and a Threshold-Based Pruning strategy, effectively capturing combinatorial peer synergy while reducing computational complexity. An optional Novelty-Weighted Online Adaptation module with Momentum-based updates enables nodes to internalize collaborative knowledge after interaction while filtering gradient noise derived from fluctuating peer qualities. Theoretical analysis characterizes wireless latency and outage feasibility, amortized communication tradeoffs against PEFT-based FL, sequence-level privacy leakage, and convergence under stated assumptions. Extensive experiments on standard NLU and knowledge-intensive benchmarks demonstrate that CITE reduces communication overhead while outperforming state-of-the-art federated baselines in inference accuracy and privacy resilience.
10.1109/tits.2026.3731813: Anomaly detection in vehicular communication is critical for ensuring the safety of the Internet of Vehicles (IoV). Although deep learning methods have achieved strong performance, their deployment is limited by privacy concerns and centralized data collection. Federated learning (FL) provides a privacy-preserving solution, but its effectiveness is often degraded by non-IID data, resource constraints, and unstable client participation. To address these challenges, we propose FedUCANet-MoE, a lightweight personalized federated learning framework for in-vehicle anomaly detection. First, we design UCANet, a compact model based on the Universal Inverted Bottleneck (UIB), enabling efficient feature extraction under resource constraints. Then, we introduce a mixture-of-experts (MoE) mechanism that adaptively fuses a global model and a locally specialized model through a lightweight router, achieving sample-level personalization. Experiments on two CAN bus datasets, Car-Hacking and CICIoV2024, demonstrate that UCANet achieves over 99% accuracy with only 1.8M parameters and 0.7ms inference latency, significantly outperforming existing lightweight models. Furthermore, FedUCANet-MoE consistently outperforms FedAvg, local fine-tuning, FedProx, and Ditto under various non-IID settings and partial client participation scenarios. These results indicate that the proposed framework effectively balances global generalization and local specialization, providing a practical and robust solution for privacy-preserving anomaly detection in IoV systems. The source code of this study is available athttps://github.com/chng2504/FedUCANet-MoE
10.1109/tmm.2026.3729110: Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning framework that enhances privacy and data security. However, model parameters communicated between the central server and local clients are still vulnerable to gradient leakage attacks (GLA), where attackers can fully reconstruct the local training data, posing serious privacy risks. To defend against such attacks, differential privacy is commonly used to provide privacy guarantees for FL, but this often comes at the cost of substantial performance degradation. To address this challenge, we explore GLA from a novel perspective of channels and, through comprehensive experiments, discover that using only partial channel information from certain parameters, rather than complete information from all channels, is sufficient to recover original images. Further analysis validates that the channel information in shared parameters is critical, with its amount directly determining the success of the attack. Based on this insight, we propose FedLCP, a lightweight channel-level privacy protection method. It leverages the trace of the empirical Fisher information matrix to estimate the information contained in each parameter channel and injects adaptive channel-level noise, effectively defending against both GLA and our newly explored channel-level attacks. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis for the convergence of FL when applying our method. Extensive experiments conducted on three datasets demonstrate that FedLCP not only provides privacy protection comparable to differential privacy but also achieves significant accuracy improvements, with excellent convergence and only a slight impact on computational costs.
10.1109/tai.2026.3734019: The federated learning (FL) technique was developed to mitigate data privacy issues in the traditional machine learning paradigm. While FL ensures that a user's data always remain with the user, the gradients are shared with the centralized server to build the global model. This results in privacy leakage, where the server can infer private information from the shared gradients. To mitigate this flaw, the next-generation FL architectures proposed encryption and anonymization techniques to protect the model updates from the server. However, this approach creates other challenges, such as malicious users sharing false gradients. Since the gradients are encrypted, the server is unable to identify rogue users. To mitigate both attacks, this paper proposes a novel FL algorithm based on a fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) scheme. We develop a distributed multi-key additive homomorphic encryption scheme that supports model aggregation in FL. We also develop a novel aggregation scheme within the encrypted domain, utilizing users' non-poisoning rates, to effectively address data poisoning attacks while ensuring privacy is preserved by the proposed encryption scheme. Rigorous security, privacy, convergence, and experimental analyses have been provided to show that FheFL is novel, secure, and private, and achieves comparable accuracy at reasonable computational cost.
10.1109/tpds.2026.3733479: In a federated learning environment with heterogeneous, limited and time-varying computational resource capabilities, it is challenging to update deep neural network in real-time. To address this challenge, we propose FedAD, an adaptive block-dropping approach for federated learning on resource-constrained devices. FedAD dynamically adjusts the size of the local training model in real-time by dropping blocks based on the device’s varying resource availability. This is controlled by a policy network, which determines the drop probability for each block depending on data inputs. Using the policy network’s output, FedAD generates a drop policy that decides which blocks in the neural network are dropped during local training. Applying this method, each device can independently generate the drop policy that dynamically adapts to the input and real-time available resources. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedAD converges faster and outperforms state-of-the-art methods in resource-constrained settings, performing on par with or better (between 10% to 50%) than baselines in resource-rich environments. Additionally, FedAD demonstrates strong adaptability to real-time resource fluctuations and high flexibility in accommodating heterogeneous resources.
10.1109/tnnls.2026.3722372: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered heart sound auscultation offers a noninvasive and accessible approach for diagnosing cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). However, training robust diagnostic models requires large-scale data, which is hindered by strict privacy regulations across isolated medical institutions. While federated learning (FL) addresses privacy concerns, real-world medical data exhibits severe non-independent and non-identically (Non-IID) characteristics, including label heterogeneity, intraclass representation diversity, and interclass imbalance. Existing FL methods primarily focus on personalized client models and struggle to construct a comprehensive global model capable of recognizing all disease subtypes under such extreme data heterogeneity. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel two-stage decoupled federated prototype learning framework. In the first stage, we introduce a multicluster trainable prototype aggregation mechanism equipped with comprehensive local feature space calibration-incorporating $L_{2}$ normalization, learnable prototype radii, multilevel alignment, and adversarial domain adaptation-to dynamically handle label skew and intraclass diversity. In the second stage, we design a decoupled joint training paradigm that reconstructs a unified global classifier through privacy-preserving one-shot feature sharing and prior-based logit adjustment. Comprehensive experiments on the Yaseen valvular heart diseases (VHDs) and ZCHSound congenital heart diseases (CHDs) datasets demonstrate the advantages of our method. Specifically, our framework effectively narrows extreme performance disparities among individual client models and successfully constructs a robust, reusable global model that outperforms traditional centralized and federated baselines under severe class imbalance, all while ensuring minimal communication overhead.
10.1109/tc.2026.3732800: Microservice (MS) architecture breaks down an application into lightweight service modules, making it an ideal choice for delivering complex applications in resource-constrained mobile edge computing (MEC) networks. This paper studies an Edge Micro-Service (EdgeMS) platform with a specific focus on EdgeMS deployment. EdgeMS deployment refers to installing MS modules at geo-distributed edge servers and enables cross-site function calls to accomplish the full functionalities. This problem is particularly challenging due to the inexplicit impact of disunified platform configurations, the complicated interactions of MS modules over dynamic MEC networks, and the deployment coupling across edge servers. We propose a novel algorithm called Distributed Graph Reinforcement Learning (DGRL) to handle the above unique challenges. DGRL employs the reinforcement learning framework that learns an EdgeMS deployment policy by directly interacting with the EdgeMS platform, thereby avoiding inaccurate characterizations of various influencing factors under disunified platform configurations. DGRL embeds graph neural networks as its learning engine, enabling it to capture complicated interactions between MS modules over dynamic edge networks. Particularly, DGRL designs a novel mechanism to realize distributed inference and training of GNNs, making it possible to generate site-wise deployment policies and drastically improve the scalability for coupled decision-making. We evaluate the performance of DGRL on a realistic MEC network topology, utilizing real-world MS applications, and compare it against state-of-the-art learning strategies in both centralized and distributed settings. The results demonstrate that DGRL reduces the data transmission delay and computing delay 24.58× and 10.19×, respectively, during learning, while maintaining performance comparable to centralized learning. Additionally, DGRL exhibits superior scalability compared to federated learning.
10.1109/tnsm.2026.3732465: Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a key enabler for privacy-preserving, decentralized sensing systems, giving rise to Federated Mobile Crowdsensing (F-MCS). A well-known bottleneck in such systems is the inefficiency of synchronous training, which stalls for all participants and is susceptible to stragglers in heterogeneous environments. Although asynchronous FL methods have been explored to alleviate this, they often introduce the critical issue of stale updates, which can degrade model convergence and accuracy. To simultaneously address the challenges of efficiency, staleness, and robustness, this paper proposes a novel Dropout-Tolerant Privacy Aggregation (DTPA) scheme for FL that operates without a trusted third party (TTP). Our solution leverages the distributed decryption feature of the lifted EC-ElGamal cryptosystem to enable secure, decentralized model aggregation. We further introduce an efficient worker selection algorithm to systematically reduce waiting time. Moreover, a dedicated dropout-tolerant mechanism is developed to maintain protocol execution even under a high rate of client failures, thereby enhancing robustness. Security analysis confirms that our scheme fulfills essential privacy and security requirements. Extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed DTPA scheme significantly improves training efficiency and convergence stability compared to state-of-the-art methods, while remaining practical for deployment on resource-constrained mobile devices.
10.1109/tii.2026.3726678: Mechanical fault diagnosis has become critical with the growing complexity and automation of industrial systems. In practical scenarios, fault data are often distributed across decentralized clients with heterogeneous data distributions and privacy constraints, while different clients may adopt different model architectures due to deployment-specific requirements. Federated learning (FL) facilitates collaborative model training across decentralized clients without sharing raw data; however, standard parameter-aggregation-based FL generally relies on architectural consistency across clients, which is difficult to satisfy in model-heterogeneous mechanical fault diagnosis. To address this problem, this article proposes federated distilled data aggregation with proxy-based tridirectional training (FedDDA-P3T) for model-heterogeneous federated fault diagnosis. More specifically, each client independently distills its local dataset into a compact distilled dataset and uploads it to the server. The distilled data are not used merely as compact substitutes for local datasets; instead, they serve as model-agnostic knowledge carriers and are aggregated on the server to support knowledge transfer across heterogeneous client models. Moreover, the server-aggregated distilled data are redistributed to clients as shared training anchors. A proxy model is further introduced to bridge heterogeneous private models through these shared anchors, forming a proxy-based tridirectional training strategy. Experiments on mechanical fault diagnosis datasets demonstrate that FedDDA-P3T achieves superior diagnostic performance over representative state-of-the-art FL methods under model-heterogeneous settings.
10.1109/tmm.2026.3733012: With the rapid development of remote sensing technology, the joint classification of hyperspectral image (HSI) and light detection and ranging (LiDAR) data has been widely studied. However, in real-world scenarios, multi-modality data are typically distributed across different platforms, making centralized training infeasible due to privacy constraints and communication costs. Moreover, obtaining sufficient labeled samples remains a major challenge. To address these issues, we propose a Shared-Specific Feature Decoupling-based Semi-Supervised Vertical Federated Learning Framework (S$^{2}$F) for HSI and LiDAR classification, which effectively exploits overlapping samples across clients to improve the classification performance under limited labeled overlapping samples without exchanging raw data. Specifically, we design the Cross-Client Self-Supervised Learning module to leverage overlapping samples and disentangle modality-shared and modality-specific features to enhance the representation capability while preserving critical information of each modality. Additionally, we propose a Dual Graph Neural Network-based Feature Aggregation module, which aggregates superpixel-level features across clients based on soft linkages and supplements them with pixel-level details through GraphSAGE. Our method only requires the exchange of superpixel intermediate features, avoiding raw data or gradient transmission, thereby ensuring privacy and reducing communication overhead. Experimental results on three public datasets demonstrate that the S$^{2}$F framework achieves accurate joint classification.
10.1109/tcad.2026.3732596: Privacy boundaries among intellectual property (IP) vendors make conventional centralized Network-on-Chip (NoC) mapping difficult to apply to heterogeneous chiplet-based DSP platforms. The problem is further complicated by non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) design preferences, strict bandwidth and timing constraints, and the large discrete search space arising from energy-latency trade-offs. This paper presents FedMap, a federated deep reinforcement learning approach that separates centralized environment simulation from decentralized policy optimization. Under a trusted-coordinator threat model, participating vendors retain proprietary communication graphs, task information, and traffic characteristics locally, while model updates are protected through gradient clipping, local noise perturbation, and secure aggregation. To improve mapping efficiency, FedMap incorporates a preference-conditioned graph hierarchical Actor-Critic (PC-GAC), which exploits communication dependencies and decomposes the original decision space while adapting to different energy-latency preferences. In addition, a preference-clustered, contribution-aware aggregation strategy (PC²-Agg) is developed to mitigate instability caused by heterogeneous client objectives and constraint conditions. Evaluations on real-time heterogeneous DSP mapping tasks show that FedMap consistently achieves better solutions than representative state-of-the-art approaches. It decreases communication cost, communication energy, and average network latency by 40.95%, 41.38%, and 39.10%, respectively. The framework also maintains stable mapping performance as system scale increases and constraints become more stringent, demonstrating its potential for privacy-preserving collaborative NoC optimization.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3732331: LoRA-based federated fine-tuning allows clients to fine-tune LoRA adapters locally and aggregates updates on the server, thereby enabling the efficient adaptation of global foundation models to distributed, domain-specific data. However, existing methods assume identical and static LoRA adapters across clients, which not only limits the utilization of heterogeneous resources and adaptation to diverse data distributions, but also prevents dynamic adjustment to clients' evolving local fine tuning state. They also struggle to achieve precise and lightweight aggregation of LoRA matrices, hindering learning performance in resource-constrained environments. To address these issues, we propose AFLoRA, an adaptive LoRA-based resource-efficient federated fine-tuning framework. For effectively adapting to Non IID local data while minimizing resource consumption, AFLoRA introduces diagonal-based dynamic rank assignment, which dynamically adjusts local LoRA ranks based on client resources and local adaptation state guided by a learnable diagonal matrix. It further decouples LoRA matrices updates between clients and the server to reduce overhead, and develops a zero-padding based rank-aware aggregation mechanism to accurately integrate heterogeneous updates through lossless matrix expansion and rank-aware weighting. These mechanisms enable AFLoRA to balance resource efficiency and fine-tuning performance effectively. Extensive experiments demonstrate that AFLoRA outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both LLM adaptation performance and fine-tuning efficiency in heterogeneous environments.
10.1109/tcc.2026.3732546: Vehicular edge computing reduces transmission latency by moving computing resources closer to vehicles. Federated learning further limits raw-data transmission by enabling local model training and uploading only model updates. However, uploaded updates remain vulnerable to model inversion or membership inference attacks by honest-but-curious servers or external adversaries. Moreover, conventional differential privacy (DP) assigns a uniform privacy budget across tasks, failing to accommodate the diverse priorities and privacy requirements of vehicular applications and potentially degrading model utility for less-sensitive tasks. To address these issues, we propose a client selection and resource allocation strategy integrating federated learning with Vehicular Edge Computing, aiming to reduce system processing latency and energy consumption while preserving the user privacy. First, we formulate the client selection and resource allocation decision problem as a Markov decision process. The formulation considers task completion, latency, energy consumption, and model accuracy, while privacy protection is enforced by priority-conditioned DP. Task priority is used to calibrate the privacy budget of uploaded updates, and Laplace perturbation is applied after update clipping. FL_MADDPG is then used to learn adaptive client selection and resource allocation policies in dynamic vehicular environments. Experiments on multiple datasets show that the proposed framework reduces latency and energy consumption compared with representative DRL baselines while maintaining model utility under differentiated privacy protection.
10.1109/tii.2026.3725678: Collaborative optimization in multimicrogrid systems (MMSs) is critical for enhancing operational efficiency, yet it is often challenged by excessive conservatism in traditional robust optimization, prohibitive communication payload, and privacy vulnerabilities in standard federated learning. To address these issues, this article proposes a novel privacy-preserving collaborative optimization framework integrating generative federated learning (GFed) with Stackelberg game theory. A time-varying weight uncertainty set is constructed to adaptively characterize wind power fluctuations, so as to mitigate overconservatism. For secure global coordination, a GFed mechanism is introduced where each microgrid locally trains its own denoising diffusion probabilistic model and uploads the preserved local generative parameters together with low-dimensional statistical features to the distribution system operator (DSO). The DSO aggregates these parameters and performs conditional reverse sampling to synthesize personalized proxy responses. The DSO-MMSs interaction is formulated as a Stackelberg game and transformed into a mathematical program with equilibrium constraints via Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions to attain an optimal collaborative equilibrium. Extensive simulations on the IEEE 69-bus system demonstrate that the proposed scheme drastically reduces the online collaborative communication payload compared with existing privacy-preserving algorithms. It decreases reconstruction attack success rates by 55.6%, 55.0%, and 21.3% over FedAvg, loosely coupled federated learning, and differential privacy-alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), respectively, with the membership inference area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) remaining close to the 0.5 random inference baseline. Meanwhile, the proposed framework attains a desirable balance among privacy security, economic performance, and computation efficiency.
10.1109/tdsc.2026.3732521: The rapid growth of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in edge computing environments has accelerated the adoption of federated learning (FL) for privacy-preserving model training. However, conventional FL frameworks remain vulnerable to single-point failures and model poisoning, while existing blockchain-based FL schemes often introduce high communication overhead in large-scale edge systems. To address these challenges, this paper proposesRBHFL-aRobustBlockchain-securedHierarchicalFederatedLearningframework tailored for edge computing. RBHFL employs a two-layer architecture: devices perform vanilla FL with their edge server in the lower layer, while a permissioned blockchain coordinates and audits server-layer aggregation in the upper layer. Specifically, aBlockchain-Secured Global Model Aggregation (BSGMA)mechanism integrates aBlockchain Data Model, anAuditor-Guided Model Validationprocess, and aProof-of-Integrity (PoI)consensus to enhance security. Through these mechanisms, model parameters, validation results, and reputation updates are immutably recorded on-chain, enabling transparent auditing and traceability of malicious participants. Extensive experiments show that RBHFL achieves strong resilience against Byzantine corruption and various poisoning attacks, accurately identifies compromised participants, and maintains accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art robust FL methods such as Krum and Trimmed Mean, while reducing total training time by up to 41.28%.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3732040: Rapid and precise semantic segmentation of flash floods, such as landslides and debris flows, is critical for emergency response and post-disaster assessment. In recent years, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) swarms offer flexible large-area coverage but face two major challenges for collaborative model training: (i) highly non-Independent and Identically Distributed (non-IID) data distributions that degrade global accuracy, and (ii) prohibitive communication costs in mobile ad hoc networks. To address these challenges, we proposeFederated Multi-Level Knowledge Distillation (FedMLKD), a novel framework that enables UAVs to exchange both logits and adaptively pooled intermediate features. This design preserves critical spatial structure while drastically reducing transmission overhead. A client quality–aware aggregation strategy further ensures robust global knowledge construction. Experiments on the Landslide segmentation dataset demonstrate that compared to state-of-the-art baselines, FedMLKD improves mIoU by 9.19% and the average Boundary F1-score by 85.54%, while reducing communication cost by nearly 200 times. These results highlight FedMLKD's ability to balance accuracy and efficiency, making it a practical candidate for real-time disaster mapping in bandwidth-constrained UAV swarms.
10.1109/tkde.2026.3731520: Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) enables participants with different feature sets but common identifiers to collaboratively train a model by sharing deep feature representations. In VFL, participants first align their data and then use the aligned samples for collaborative training. As a result, the size of the aligned dataset directly influences the performance of the federated model. However, in practice, aligned data is generally limited, particularly in multi-party scenarios, which restricts the potential of federated training. In this paper, we propose Nunchaku, a VFL framework that incorporates semi-aligned samples into federated training to enhance model performance. Semi-alignment refers to the process, if one party's dataset lacks a matching sample for a given sample from another party (i.e., one with the same ID), it identifies the most similar sample from its own dataset. This is achieved by “guessing” a sample that shares the same label and has the closest feature embedding distance to the missing sample, which is then used for alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Nunchaku significantly improves the performance of the federated model when compared to advanced baselines, across different numbers of aligned samples and various data distributions.
10.1109/tia.2026.3731545: The integration of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in active distribution networks (ADNs) requires reliable communication networks that connect distributed energy resources (DERs) to distribution system operators (DSOs). This paper presents a co-simulation framework that combines parallelized BESS scheduling optimization, packet-level communication network modeling, and DSO supervisory commands to evaluate power–communication inter-dependencies across multi-community ADNs. The framework integrates a scalable OpenDSS-PM power distribution system model, an OMNeT++/INET communication network emulator, and a DSO federate, coupled through HELICS using a lightweight DNP3-over-TCP/IP protocol to enable time-stamped measurement and command signal exchanges. A community-level BESS scheduling approach is utilized to determine optimal charge/discharge setpoints for peak demand shaving. The framework is evaluated under three scenarios on a modified IEEE 13- bus test feeder: ideal communications, shared-network congestion, and contingency event operation. Results demonstrate how communication latency, throughput limitations, and channel utilization affect BESS scheduling, supervisory command signal responsiveness, and the overall reliable operation of the ADN. The framework enables utilities and researchers to assess communication-aware BESS scheduling strategies, exploring infrastructure requirements, and enhancing ADN operation under realistic communication network conditions.
10.1109/tcomm.2026.3731795: Federated learning (FL) can safeguard the data privacy for air-ground networks, while simultaneously transmitting and reflecting reconfigurable intelligent surface (STAR-RIS) can help further enhance its channel quality. However, the model exchanges in FL may be detected by wardens, and air-ground links increase this threat. In this paper, we investigate a STAR-RIS aided air-ground covert FL scheme to hide the presence of uploading, where the unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) acts as an aerial server to collect local models from the distributed devices. To alleviate the communication burden, each device prunes the local model before transmitting. The minimum detection error probability at the warden is derived with the optimal detection threshold, indicating the worst case for the legitimate covert FL. Then, we analyze the convergence of the proposed FL scheme and provide an upper bound on the expected convergence gap of global loss function. To improve the learning performance, the convergence gap is minimized subject to the covertness and latency constraints. Specifically, the closed-forms of optimal pruning ratio and transmit power are derived, while the phase shifts of STAR-RIS and UAV position can be optimized by semidefinite relaxation and successive convex approximation, respectively. Finally, the overall problem can be solved via an alternative algorithm. Numerical results validate that the proposed covert air-ground FL scheme can achieve excellent test accuracy and convergence performance while guaranteeing the covertness assisted by STAR-RIS.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3731388: Despite the rapid progress of federated learning (FL) for mobile and edge intelligence, the reliability of on-device federated models remains largely underexplored. This gap becomes critical in distributed mobile systems where clients are resource- and bandwidth-constrained, data are highly non-IID, and training suffers from intermittent participation and stragglers. In such settings, we systematically revisit FL from a reliability standpoint and identify an underappreciated failure mode: federated models often become poorly calibrated and unreliable in uncertainty estimation, which directly compromises risk-sensitive edge decisions. Through theoretical analysis, we further reveal that this degradation mainly arises from the classifier head, where biased local priors distort the global prediction confidence. To address this issue, we first proposeAssembled Projection Heads (APH), a plug-and-play and communication-free head-ensemble framework that improves calibration by introducing controllable diversity while incurring negligible training and inference overhead. Building upon this, we developLow-Rank Adaptation (LoRA)-based APH (LoRAPH), which replaces full projection heads with low-rank counterparts, effectively reducing storage overhead for large-scale distributed clients while further enhancing uncertainty reliability. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks and FL frameworks demonstrate that APH and LoRAPH consistently improve calibration and robustness under non-IID data and partial participation, with minimal computation and communication overhead, making them practical for reliability-critical federated learning in distributed mobile systems. Notably,LoRAPHdelivers reliable uncertainty estimation with only0.34%extra training cost, near-zero inference overhead after pre-aggregation, and4.37%footprint increase, making it well-suited for bandwidth- and memory-constrained mobile deployments.
10.1109/tmc.2026.3731148: Federated learning (FL) has expanded the scope of distributed machine learning by training a global model through the amalgamation of knowledge from various distributed clients. However, the challenge of non-i.i.d. local datasets among clients introduces statistical heterogeneity, thereby compromising the performance of a single global model. Personalized federated learning (PFL) seeks to mitigate this issue by training individualized models tailored for each client. Despite the improved performance achieved by PFL, current approaches lack interpretability in quantifying the significance of inter-client contributions. Furthermore, they often pursue individual models at clients while performing model aggregation to obtain a single global model at the FL server, which still struggles to effectively capture the distinctions among clients. In response to these problems, we propose thepersonalizedFederated learning withTransparentInter-clientContribution (pFedTIC.) approach. Specifically, pFedTIC. embraces a dual-level personalized model aggregation strategy to derive an individualized model for each client, and assesses inter-client contribution with the aggregation weights for enhancing transparency. It conducts model aggregation at both the server and client sides using the similarity of model parameters and learning representations, mutual contributions between clients, and model performance. Theoretical analyses are derived to establish the non-convex convergence rate of pFedTIC.. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate its superiority over competitive methods, affirming its effectiveness in handling data heterogeneity. Moreover, the experiments also showcase its capability to interpret inter-client contributions, fostering more transparent FL collaborations.
10.1109/tnsm.2026.3731410: The Internet of Things (IoT) connects diverse, resource-constrained devices, driving innovation in domains such as healthcare, smart cities, and industrial automation. However, the exponential growth of IoT devices poses critical challenges in data processing, privacy, security, and latency. Fog Computing (FC) mitigates these issues by decentralizing computational resources, processing and storing data locally to enable low-latency, high-quality services. This makes FC an ideal platform for integrating Federated Learning (FL), a decentralized machine learning paradigm that trains models locally on IoT devices and shares only aggregated updates, preserving data privacy. Since its introduction, FL has garnered considerable attention for enabling privacy-preserving collaborative model training in distributed environments. The convergence of IoT, FC, and FL offers substantial opportunities to advance IoT system performance, but it also presents challenges in resource allocation, security, energy efficiency, computational complexity, and system heterogeneity. This survey provides a comprehensive and up-to-date analysis of the integration of FL and FC within IoT environments, exploring their synergies, challenges, and state-of-the-art advancements.We review critical aspects, including infrastructure enhancements, security mechanisms, and the emerging role of Digital Twin (DT) technology, which creates virtual replicas of IoT devices to optimize system efficiency and real-time performance. Through case studies in healthcare and smart cities, we highlight practical applications of FL-FC integration. We compare our work with existing surveys, highlight its specific focus on the FL-FC-IoT-DT convergence, and identify open challenges and future research directions toward secure, scalable, and intelligent IoT ecosystems.
10.1109/tnsm.2026.3731093: The emergence of fifth-generation (5G) and open radio access network (O-RAN) architectures has expanded the attack surface for cyber threats, creating an urgent need for enhanced and proactive mitigation strategies to ensure the preservation of quality of service (QoS), network reliability, and user data privacy in highly distributed and virtualized environments. In this context, we introduce FML-AD, a federated learning framework with meta-model refinement for adaptive attack duration prediction without centralizing raw training traffic. The proposed method combines a FLAD-trained Transformer for distributed temporal learning with an XGBoost-based second-level regression model that refines the initial predictions using controlled O-RAN testbed examples, thereby reducing prediction errors associated with the benchmark-to-deployment distribution shift. Extensive evaluation on the CICIoT2023 dataset shows that FML-AD improves prediction accuracy compared with conventional centralized and federated baselines. Furthermore, an evaluation on a controlled 5G O-RAN testbed involving ten TCP SYN and UDP flooding scenarios provides a proof-of-concept demonstration of the feasibility of the proposed post-detection prediction pipeline in the evaluated configuration. A separate exploratory transfer-learning assessment using 5G V2X radio-jamming scenarios and leave-one-scenario-out (LOSO) validation further examines whether the duration-prediction pipeline can be adapted to a different disruption mechanism under limited target-domain data. For the considered jamming configurations, several operating points in the early 3–5 sec range also produce favorable prediction results, providing preliminary evidence of transferability.
10.1109/tce.2026.3731384: Recently, a number of Heterogeneous Federated Learning (HtFL) methods have been proposed to address the problems of data and model heterogeneity using prototypes. However, the prototypes learned by individual clients may be unreliable, and simple server-side averaging may propagate such unreliability to the aggregated prototypes, which would significantly affect the efficacy of global prototypes. To solve this problem, a new HtFL method using reliable prototypes with graph neural networks, named FedRG, is proposed. FedRG assigns distinct reliability aggregation weights to client prototypes and then accordingly constructs their prototype subgraphs. After that, a graph neural network is used to optimize the collaborative relationships among clients within each subgraph, enabling the aggregation of personalized prototypes for local feature alignment. Therefore, FedRG can maintain reliable global information for each client while mitigating feature misalignment. Experiments on a large number of heterogeneous models demonstrate that FedRG achieves the best accuracy in most experimental settings, while still maintaining the communication and privacy advantages of prototype-based HtFL. The code is available at https://github.com/maker27-z/FedRG.
